sources.news_title: Focus turns to general election as Markey and Deaton face off for Senate
sources.text:
The Massachusetts primary is in the past, and it's onto the general election for Democratic Sen. Ed Markey and GOP challenger John Deaton.
The pair each claimed their party's nomination on Tuesday. Deaton ran unopposed in the Republican primary, while Markey defeated an opponent in Rep. Seth Moulton.
Stream NBC10 Boston news for free, 24/7, wherever you are.
After the high-profile Democratic primary, Deaton is eager to make the case of why he should be the state's next U.S. senator.
"If they really want change, if they want someone who's going to be a disruptor, then they should give me a really serious look," he said Wednesday.
Markey began the general election campaign by attempting to tie Deaton to President Donald Trump.
"Massachusetts does not want to have a MAGA Republican representing them in the Senate," said Markey. "A vote to confirm Supreme Court justices that Trump might nominate, cabinet officers that Trump might nominate."
"My challenge is reaching those folks, and he's hoping that by calling me MAGA, or calling me a Trumper, that people will tune me out," Deaton said. "But we're doing a lot of microtargeting across the state."
Deaton will need to walk a tight rope with Democratic, Republican and unenrolled voters. During a town hall on Wednesday, he made clear where he stood on Trump, maintaining he has not voted for Trump in 2016, 2020 or 2024.
"This may disappoint some of you, but you're stuck with me now," he said during the event in Quincy.
Beyond that debate, both candidates are laying out their policy priorities.
"I have real solutions on energy, housing, health care, education," said Deaton.
"I ran on Medicare for all, I ran on the Green New Deal, I ran on taxing millionaires and billionaires," Markey said.
Wednesday showed an early look at each candidate's strategy as they look ahead to November.
"They want fundamental change in the direction of this country," said Markey.
"People aren't looking for ideology today, they're looking for solutions," said Deaton.
The general election will be held Nov. 3, with early voting beginning on Oct. 17 and running through Oct. 30.

sources.news_title: Established Incumbent Triumphs Over Challenging ‘Rising Star’ in Primary
sources.text:
In a key primary yesterday, U.S. Senator Ed Markey triumphed over U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton in the Massachusetts Democratic primary for the Senate seat. This race showcased the strength of incumbency, as Markey, a seasoned politician, held his ground against Moulton, who was thought to be a rising star.
Despite Moulton’s efforts and aspirations, the election results underscore how challenging it is for newcomers to unseat a long-standing figure in the political landscape. Many observers had their eyes on this match-up, speculating on the potential for a shakeup in the Democratic Party.
The Implications of Incumbency
The results serve as a reminder that experience and established voter relationships often hold significant sway in elections. Markey’s victory reaffirms traditional political dynamics where incumbents typically dominate these crucial races.
This outcome leaves supporters of both candidates pondering the future direction of the Democratic Party in Massachusetts and beyond as they evaluate the implications of this high-profile election.

NEW: Dem ‘Rising Star’ Loses Primary Bid Against Longtime Incumbent
Incumbent U.S. Senator Ed Markey defeated U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton in the Massachusetts Democratic primary for U.S. Senate on Tuesday night.
Notable forecasters such as the Associated Press and Decision Desk HQ called the race approximately 30 minutes after polls closed. With more than 95 percent of votes reported, Markey received 571,246 votes, or 64.8 percent, while Moulton received 309,870 votes, or 35.2 percent, according to results compiled by The New York Times.
Markey, 80, has served in Congress since 1976, first in the House and then in the Senate after winning a 2013 special election. Moulton, 47 has been seen as a “rising star” in Massachusetts Democratic Party politics over his six terms in the U.S. House.

Moulton centered his campaign on generational change, stating that Markey was too old to seek another term that would end when Markey would be 86. “Is he too old? Look, every political consultant will tell me not to say this, but the honest truth is, yes,” the congressman told the Boston Globe. “I think that we need to learn the lessons of Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Dianne Feinstein and Joe Biden,” he added.
Markey emphasized his legislative record, including co-sponsorship of the Green New Deal and support for Medicare for All. He received endorsements from Senators Bernie Sanders (I-VT) and Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and Ayanna Pressley (D-MA), and groups such as the Sunrise Movement.
As for Moulton, he received support from some moderate Democrats and veterans’ organizations, including VoteVets. Moulton and allied groups spent $7.1 million on advertising, compared with $3.9 million spent by Markey and his allies, according to AdImpact.
Policy differences were limited, though Markey zeroed in on Moulton’s 2024 comments on transgender athletes in girls’ sports. Moulton had said he did not want his daughters “getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete.”
He later apologized after backlash from the party’s far-left, stating thathe was “sorry if my comments hurt you.” Markey frequently criticized the remarks during the campaign.
“Massachusetts needs a senator who stands up and fights back, a senator who never forgets who they are fighting for. That has been the mission of my life, and it always will be,” Markey said following his victory. He also described the result as a “testament to the power of the progressive movement” and added, “That fight is in our hands here in Massachusetts, in Maine, in Michigan. Our progressive movement knows how to fight. We cannot surrender tomorrow.”
Markey is almost certain to win re-election in November due to Massachusetts’ deep blue partisan lean.

sources.news_title: Democrat who pandered to anti-trans beliefs is thrashed in primary
sources.text:
Democratic Sen. Ed Markey romped to victory in his Massachusetts primary against Rep. Seth Moulton on Tuesday night, marking a win for a longtime champion of transgender rights over a Democrat who had questioned whether the party should defend those rights.
Markey won by over 29 percentage points, with 98% of the expected vote reporting. He is heavily favored to win the general election against the Republican nominee, John Deaton.
Much of the mainstream media coverage of the race has focused on the age of the candidates. Markey is 80, and Moulton is 47. But unlike some other primary races in which age and association with the Democratic establishment has been an issue, the Massachusetts primary race focused candidates’ willingness to defend progressive values, like trans rights, as a major issue.
After former Vice President Kamala Harris lost the 2024 presidential election to Donald Trump, with Trump having repeatedly attacked her over support for trans rights, Moulton floated the idea of Democrats retreating in their support for equality.
“I have two little girls, I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete, but as a Democrat I’m supposed to be afraid to say that,” Moulton told The New York Times in November 2024, referring to trans children participating in school sports—an issue Trump and his allies like Fox News regularly demagogued.
In his race this year against Markey, Moulton tried to walk back those comments, which attracted widespread condemnation, but Markey continually criticized him over his willingness to abandon defending a vulnerable minority. In a primary debate between the two last month, Markey said that Moulton “threw those kids under the political bus after the election.”
He added, “We should have been loving those kids. We should have been protecting them against Trump, against Fox, against the MAGA base that we’re just trying to demonize and take advantage of all these trans kids.”
Markey has been a longtime advocate for trans equality, and his refusal to fall in line with Democrats who are willing to bend on the issue led to strong support in the primary from LGBTQ+ groups as well as a clear majority of the Democratic electorate.
Markey’s continued support for trans rights comes as they have been under assault by Trump and other Republicans. The right has tried to roll back trans rights, including by banning them from serving in the military, and it is even trying to prevent hospitals from providing gender-affirming care.
Clearly, Massachusetts Democrats had little interest in backing a politician who, while not being an open bigot like figures on the right, nonetheless gave credence to those same bigoted stances.
The Democratic Party is having a strong internal debate about age and willingness to fight for progressive ideas. In the case of Markey, the choice was overwhelming in favor of an older Democrat who refused to yield on a core issue of basic humanity and equality.

sources.news_title: Seth Moulton Sold Out Trans Kids — and Lost His Senate Race
sources.text:
Massachusetts Sen. Ed Markey comfortably defeated Rep. Seth Moulton in his Democratic Senate primary on Tuesday, in what the media — and Moulton himself — had described as a “generational” challenge.
The framing is understandable: In a country suffering under gerontocratic rule, Markey is 80 and Moulton is 47.
Age, however, was the least of what was at stake in Moulton’s run from the decaying center of the Democratic Party. Moulton ran on a conservative line, recycling right-wing talking points and echoing Donald Trump to suggest, erroneously, that Democrats have been failing because they have not been conservative enough.
Markey may be 80 years old, but his campaign did precisely what Democrats must if they want to appeal to progressives and bring in a broad working-class voter base: He ran on issues of economic inequality, taxing billionaires, green energy, and universal health care — all while refusing to jettison support for vulnerable minorities, especially trans people.
Meanwhile Moulton, claiming to represent a break in the status quo, repeated precisely the tired centrist playbook that has both failed America’s multiracial working class and failed to win elections. He punched left and, as Markey himself highlighted, threw trans kids “under the bus.”
In a risible misreading of the Democrats’ 2024 presidential election loss, Moulton suggested that his party had shown too much care for trans rights. (It had not.)
“I have two little girls,” Moulton told the New York Times just after the November 2024 election. “I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete.”
It was only last month that Moulton offered a tempered apology for the anti-trans remarks — and only because Markey had lambasted him during a debate.
“He just took the whole playbook of MAGA and Trump, and he blamed those kids for the loss,” said Markey, who has been consistent in his advocacy for trans rights. “We should have been loving those kids. There’s only 12 trans athletes in the whole of the NCAA. We should have been embracing them.”
Indeed, we should question the validity of this so-called “debate” entirely: Why did the moderator of a Senate primary debate even feel the need to ask a question about trans girls in sports at all?
This is not, after all, a political problem in need of addressing in Massachusetts, or anywhere else. It is a ghoulish far-right panic that has been baselessly elevated into a hot-button issue, with the help of Democratic cowardice.
Fox News, of all places, noted that Markey is “one of the few Democrats running this midterm cycle who is continuing to push for transgender rights, particularly in sports” — as if that were a bad thing.
“There is good evidence that transgender issues were a major part of Markey’s victory, too,” wrote reporter and trans advocate Erin Reed. “In the final days of the campaign, a UMass/Amherst poll asked primary voters how a candidate who embraces anti-trans positions or policies would impact their vote. In that poll, a whopping 67% stated it would make their vote less likely for that candidate.”
Markey, the longtime incumbent, was already at an advantage. And no doubt proselytizers for Democratic Party conservatism will stress that Markey’s victory in deep-blue Massachusetts cannot offer lessons for Democrats running in less progressive territory. This again would be to selectively learn the wrong lessons from Kamala Harris’s spectacular 2024 failure.
It should not need repeating that Democrats in 2024 campaigned on Republican talking points, with Harris donning khaki for photo ops at the Arizona border. If Donald Trump’s campaign attacking trans people gained purchase, it is because Democrats roundly failed to answer it by demystifying right-wing anti-trans fearmongering. They also failed to offer a robust, class-focused platform to vote for.
Being nearly half someone’s age does not constitute a generational challenge; contesting the staid ways of a generational establishment does. Moulton did nothing of the sort.
Markey said it best on Tuesday: “Generational change isn’t about compromising.”

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

sources.text:
Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.
U.S. Sen. Ed Markey cruised to a decisive victory in the Democratic primary against U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton, as voters soundly rejected the Salem congressman’s effort to turn the race into a referendum on Markey’s age.
In unofficial results on Tuesday night, Markey secured roughly 70 percent among Democratic primary voters to Moulton’s 30 percent.
It marked the second consecutive race in which Markey turned back a primary challenge from a younger member of the state’s congressional delegation. Six years ago, it was 39-year-old Joe Kennedy III who failed to make the case for generational change. This time, with Markey turning 80 during the heat of the primary campaign, it was the 47-year old Moulton who waged an ultimately losing bet that the senator had finally worn out his stay.
Moulton launched his campaign last October with a simple pitch — it was time to pass the torch.
Moulton, a Marine veteran who served four tours in Iraq, argued that it was time for a generational change in leadership and that he would bring fresh energy to the fight against President Trump and his agenda.
Markey pointed to his authorship of the Green New Deal, consistent progressive bona fides, and said he had never felt more energized about a campaign. He insisted repeatedly that it was not your age but the age of your ideas that was important, and then pointed to his long record of progressive policy battles.
Every public poll of the race showed Markey comfortably ahead.
After the candidates met for their first debate on July 8, the numbers barely wavered. A Suffolk University/Boston Globe poll found a majority of voters already leaning Markey by mid-August. A WBUR/UMass Amherst survey days later had him up nearly 30 points. The final Emerson College poll in late August put Markey at 60 percent to Moulton’s 33 percent. Women and voters under 40 — the exact voters Moulton needed to peel away — broke hardest for Markey, Emerson’s pollster said.
On policy, there was often little daylight between them — a point both men conceded across three debates.
Both called themselves the true progressive in the race and both back universal health care, though not the same version. Markey has embraced Medicare for All, a single-payer system, while Moulton favors a public option that would let a government plan compete alongside private insurers. Markey has also stayed tied to the Green New Deal, which he co-authored.
A major point of contention throughout the race was Moulton’s comments about transgender athletes shortly after President Trump’s 2024 victory, in which he talked about not wanting his daughters “getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete.” That prompted an apology from Moulton on the debate stage with Markey, and the incumbent senator accusing the congressman of “throwing trans kids under the bus.”
Markey’s sound win on Tuesday further signals that voters found him to be the unalloyed progressive, with Moulton’s comments around trans issues dogging him throughout the race.
Almost all of Markey’s fellow Massachusetts Democrats in Washington closed ranks, with six of the state’s eight House members and Sen. Elizabeth Warren endorsing him. Only Reps. Stephen Lynch and Jake Auchincloss stayed neutral, The Boston Globe reported.
Moulton’s most notable institutional counterweight came from The Boston Globe, which endorsed him over Markey. He also leaned on fellow veterans-turned-politicians who he helped elect nationally, including New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill.
Throughout the campaign, Markey cited his work with progressive star Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who was a prominent Markey backer against Kennedy in 2020. She held off on endorsing this time before backing him in the race’s final week.
Moulton had unseated an incumbent before, beating then-Rep. John Tierney in 2014. But his recent efforts to crack the party’s upper echelons and comments on trans young people in sports gave Markey’s allies ammunition to paint him as a striver out of step with Massachusetts priorities. In 2018, Moulton waged a failed attempt to block Nancy Pelosi from the speakership, and he made a short-lived 2020 presidential run.
Markey is a heavy favorite in November against Republican John Deaton, a Marine veteran and cryptocurrency attorney who lost to Sen. Elizabeth Warren by about 20 points in 2024. Massachusetts hasn’t sent a Republican to the Senate since Scott Brown’s 2010 special-election win. Brown’s DC tenure was brief. Two years later, Warren defeated him.

Rep. Seth Moulton (D-MA) lost Tuesday’s U.S. Senate primary to incumbent Sen. Ed Markey (D-MA) a month after apologizing for suggesting that Democrats should moderate their support for transgender rights.
On Tuesday evening, the Associated Press called the race for Markey, with the incumbent earning 65% of the vote to Moulton’s 35%.
          
Related
Both candidates have histories of supporting LGBTQ+ rights and voting against anti-trans legislation. Moulton co-sponsored the Transgender Bill of Rights when it was introduced in 2023, as well as multiple versions of the Equality Act. He’s also maintained a score of 100 on HRC’s Congressional Scorecard, and he voted against the anti-trans “Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act” last year.
But in the wake of President Donald Trump’s victory in the 2024 presidential election, involving a vitriolic anti-trans campaign, Moulton was one of the first Democrats to suggest that support for trans rights had hurt the Democratic party — despite exit polling that indicated trans issues had little to do with Trump’s victory.

Moulton’s comments drew immediate criticism from trans advocates. Days later, he defended his statement in an interview with CNN. “I was just speaking authentically as a parent about one of many issues where Democrats are just out of touch with the majority of Americans. And I stand by my position, even though I may not have used exactly the right words,” he said, adding that while he was willing to debate the issue, those who criticized him were “more interested in shaming fellow Democrats, shaming the majority of voters, when they simply don’t meet their ideological purity test.”
After announcing his campaign for Markey’s seat in October, Moulton was booed at Boston’s October 18 No Kings Rally and again at the city’s annual Pride parade in June.
During a debate with Markey early last month, Moulton apologized for his 2024 comments.

That was not my intention,” he said. “If you’re in the trans community or you’re a trans kid feeling the weight of the Trump administration and the Supreme Court, you matter, you’re valued, and I will always have your back.”
Markey’s win on Tuesday marks another victory for the progressive wing of the Democratic Party, which has seen candidates beat more moderate opponents in some states this year. But as NPR notes, it also marks a defeat for those calling for generational change in Congress. Markey, who turned 80 in July, has been in politics since 1973 and has held his U.S. Senate seat since 2013. He is heavily favored to win in November’s general election, according to the Cook Political Report.
“Ed Markey not only proudly stood beside the trans community but campaigned on trans equality as a central issue of importance to his candidacy,” wrote trans activist Charlotte Clymer on X. “He’s now on track to win by 35+ points against an opponent nearly half his age.”
She added, “It took half an hour for Ed Markey to beat Seth Moulton on Election Night. 30 minutes. I love you, Massachusetts.”
It remains unclear whether Moulton’s loss in deep blue Massachusetts will influence how Democrats address trans rights in 2028. As independent journalist Aleksandra Vaca notes, both congressional and gubernatorial candidates in Iowa and Ohio have supported banning trans athletes from women’s and girls’ sports and locker rooms. And at least one potential 2028 Democratic presidential contender, Rahm Emanuel, has said in multiple interviews that trans rights are a distraction that could cost the party the election.

sources.news_title: Town-by-town maps: See how Markey vs. Moulton compared to Markey vs. Kennedy - The Boston Globe
sources.text:
Ed Markey tromped through Massachusetts’ Senate Democratic primary Tuesday, crushing Representative Seth Moulton in nearly every corner of the Commonwealth, unofficial results Wednesday show.
The 80-year-old incumbent carried the three largest cities — Boston, Worcester, and Springfield — by a 40-plus point margin and beat out his challenger in all but 12 Massachusetts municipalities, including in Salem, listed as Moulton’s place of residence.
It marks a victory for the longtime elected official, attacked by 47-year-old Moulton (and some voters) on the campaign trail for being too old and out of touch to retain his seat. Tuesday’s knockout even outdoes Markey’s triumph over Joseph Kennedy III in 2020.
Though Markey will face Republican nominee John Deaton this fall, he’s likely to cruise to reelection in deep-blue Massachusetts.
“Tonight is a testament to the power of the progressive movement,” Markey said in a victory speech. “We need to take back this future because it is a future that belongs to all of us.”
Markey secured the Tuesday win by appealing to Massachusetts’ liberal base and positioning his five decades in Washington against Moulton’s calls for generational change.
That message touched voters statewide.
Markey had a sizable showing in Chelsea, Lowell, and Fall River after trailing Kennedy in those “Gateway Cities” in 2020.
He once again successfully wooed voters in his hometown of Malden and longtime progressive strongholds, such as Somerville, Cambridge, and Northampton. More than 70 percent of voters in those cities sided with Markey.
Moulton, by contrast, saw his most substantial support in Marblehead, winning 60 percent of the vote. It was the only town he won by a double-digit margin as of Wednesday morning.
Moulton also prevailed by slim margins in some additional Eastern Massachusetts municipalities, such as Wellesley, Lynnfield, and Topsfield.
Southern Massachusetts turned out for Markey Tuesday after eschewing him six years ago. Voters in a band of the state, from south of Worcester through Plymouth, largely backed Kennedy in 2020, but were uninterested in Moulton.
The race was only closely contested in 18 municipalities — including Nahant, Swampscott, and Ipswich — which were split between Markey and Moulton by less than 5 percent.

sources.news_title: Old and On the Way: How Ed Markey Dispatched Seth Moulton in Massachusetts
sources.text:
Old and On the Way: How Ed Markey Dispatched Seth Moulton in Massachusetts
Moulton, a centrist opportunist, sought to unseat his incumbent opponent by posturing as a young progressive. Voters didn’t fall for it.
Massachusetts Representative Seth Moulton was the last 2020 Democratic presidential candidate to speak at the Iowa State Fair “political soapbox” in August 2019, and I got to see him there. He delivered a lackluster speech before a relatively small audience. Hilariously, he told the crowd that “I had people talking to me at the urinal in the restroom, saying that they’re here to hear my speech.” My friends and I joked that we could feel the “Moultmentum.”
To no one’s surprise, Moulton left the primary race six days later—months before any votes were cast. In 2018, he had been a leader in a small centrist Democratic movement to block Nancy Pelosi from becoming speaker if Democrats took the House back in the midterms. After the party did, that Moulton campaign also went nowhere.
Moulton’s 2026 primary challenge to Democratic Senator Ed Markey met the same fate Tuesday night, when the progressive incumbent beat him by nearly a two-to-one margin. The Boston centrist, 47, tried to make the race a generational challenge against the 80-year-old Markey. But in fact, Moulton locked himself into the role of the old and out-of-touch guy, when two days after Kamala Harris lost to Donald Trump in 2024, he unburdened himself to The New York Times and announced that he disagreed with Harris and many Democrats’ progressive views, including staunch support for trans rights. “I have two little girls,” he said. “I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete. But as a Democrat, I’m supposed to be afraid to say that.” Markey quickly denounced him for throwing trans Americans “under the bus,” but Moulton insisted he was only speaking hard truths to a complacent progressive establishment. “I think that our refusal to engage in this debate, to answer the Republicans’ attacks, did a great disservice to the trans community,” he said.
These efforts to play to anti-trans sentiment within the Democratic party fell flat in Moulton’s Senate bid. At an October “No Kings” rally in Boston, Markey drew cheers, wearing a sheer trans scarf in pink and light blue, while Moulton was booed. As his trans-baiting ploys failed to gain any traction in his Senate bid, Moulton apologized to anyone who was hurt by his remarks and said he broadly supported trans rights. Still, he never took back his slam on trans athletes’ playing in women’s sports.
That wasn’t the only reason Markey won, but it was one of them. The larger reason Moulton lost is that he is a career centrist opportunist who kicked Harris while she was down, tried to take the gavel from Pelosi, and consistently blamed the party’s left for Trump’s two victories. Challenging Markey, he also tried to revive the broadly shared Democratic discomfort, especially in hindsight, with Biden running for reelection at 80, when he was clearly hobbled in speech and physical movement by his age (and diagnosed with late-stage prostate cancer once he left office.)
Sadly for Biden, there’s no comparison with Markey, who is well-spoken, witty, and agile. The incumbent senator also put together strong support from progressives, including fellow Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren, Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, Massachusetts Representative Ayanna Presley, and New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, all of whom joined him for a late rally on Sunday. Years ago, he backed Ocasio-Cortez when the Green New Deal was considered radical (it later drove some Biden policies), and he also backs Medicare for All, expanding Social Security, and higher taxes on the wealthy.
“This is the greatest gathering of progressive voices on one stage,” Markey told the crowd on Sunday. “Our progressive-palooza. That’s what we have put together.” But the real excitement came with Tuesday’s vote-a-palooza, when he won back his seat 65–35.
Moulton drew progressive ire for linking Markey to the late sex-abuser Jeffrey Epstein, charging him with “meeting with a lobbyist on behalf of…Epstein.” Markey angrily denied the charge, which was eventually disproven. Another supposed point Moulton scored in a debate with Markey—a gotcha exchange that had Markey confessing that he wasn’t sure he’d ever used artificial intelligence—also turned out to be a nonissue. “I use whatever is inside of my iPhone and my iPad, whatever comes up,” the senator said. “And I don’t know what company my iPad might be using.” It was an honest and fair answer: None of us truly know what kind of software our devices employ. But the absolutely correct answer would have been that the Big Tech companies are putting so much AI slop in their devices and apps, it leaves users adopting AI whether they want to or not.
Despite Moulton’s slaps at Pelosi and Harris, in this race he wanted to be known as a progressive. His campaign website features a “redbox”—a ploy that campaigns use to skirt campaign rules against coordinating with outside groups by placing approved messaging for other advertising initiatives or social-media promotions to adopt within a notionally unaffiliated red frame on their websites. Moulton’’s redbox said, “Voters under 40 on the go need to see that Ed Markey willfully doesn’t understand AI and is clinging to power while AI companies go unregulated, destroying our planet, our jobs and our mental health…. [They] need to see that Seth Moulton is a next generation progressive fighter who supports abolishing ICE, taxing the rich and health care for all.”
If that sort of appeal comes off as desperate opportunism, that’s because it is. Just last year, Moulton told The Boston Globe that progressive populism is “great for Democrats if we want to continue losing.” Jonathan Cohn, policy director of Progressive Mass, denounced Moulton’s 2026 moves. “Seth has done a fascinating job of trying to rebrand himself as progressive this cycle,” Cohn told The Lever. “[Moulton] doesn’t ever really actually hit on the big problem over the past few decades of the Democratic Party’s movement away from thinking about how the government can positively intervene to improve people’s everyday lives.”
Markey’s victory surprised some people, but I wasn’t one of them. I have never considered Moulton any kind of progressive, and I remember when Markey beat former representative Joseph P. Kennedy III, scion of Massachusetts’s most powerful political dynasty. No member of the Kennedy clan had ever lost a race there before. In November, Markey faces Republican John Deaton, who in 2024 lost badly to Elizabeth Warren.

sources.news_title: Seth Moulton Abandoned Trans People, And It Cost Him Everything: Ed Markey Crushes Him In MA Senate Primary
sources.text:
The Democrat who made abandoning transgender people into the post-2024 capitulation script for "moderate" Democrats has now been abandoned himself, by the voters of his own state. Congressman Seth Moulton, the originator of the current wave of anti-transgender Democrats, blamed Democrats' 2024 defeat in part on the party's support for transgender people in the immediate aftermath of the election, fearmongering over transgender athletes and calling trans girls "male" athletes who would run over his daughters on the playing field. His remarks sparked fury in his own state, even as he opted to run for higher office, challenging Senator Ed Markey in the Massachusetts Democratic Senate primary. Rather than run away from transgender people, though, Markey used the moment to differentiate himself, championing transgender people at every turn, and the issue became a defining point of difference between the two candidates at debates and rallies. Now we have a final result: Markey has trounced Moulton, winning 65 to 35 in a race that some polls once showed as fairly close early on, and come January, Moulton will hold no elected office at all, having given up his safe House seat to run.
In 2024, in the aftermath of Kamala Harris's loss to Donald Trump, Moulton became one of the earliest to embrace a new, albeit rare, line of thinking among some Democrats: that transgender individuals were to blame for the election, and that sports bans on transgender youth are good to embrace. Such bans have come with proposals to genitally inspect student athletes, and in Utah, officials secretly investigated a girl's sex all the way back to kindergarten after the parents of the girls she had defeated complained. In an interview with The New York Times the day after Trump's victory, Moulton said, "I have two little girls, I don't want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete, but as a Democrat I'm supposed to be afraid to say that." Then, following the backlash, he doubled down in a Washington Post op-ed titled "I'm done with Democratic purity tests" and declared that "the backlash has only served to reinforce my original point."
And backlash he did receive. Immediately after his comments, his constituents pushed back: hundreds of people gathered outside his Salem office waving pride flags, demanding to be heard. "To say that his kids can get run over by people who are previously male shows not only his ignorance about what transgender is, it shows how he is willing to make the most vulnerable people in our community more vulnerable," said Ward 5 Councilor Jeff Cohen, who spoke at the rally. Not long after, organizers launched a concerted effort to primary him and remove him from office. Moulton attempted to sidestep that fight by giving up his safe House seat entirely and running for higher office instead, challenging Senator Markey, the older Democratic incumbent, for his seat. His old seat will not miss him: on the same night Moulton lost, Dan Koh won the Democratic primary to replace him. Koh, a former senior Biden White House official and chief of staff to Boston Mayor Marty Walsh, is heavily favored in November, and he pledges to "fight to ensure transgender Americans have access to healthcare, education, and safe, welcoming communities."
Immediately, transgender issues became a differentiator between the two candidates. At Boston's No Kings rally last October, Moulton was booed as he took the stage; Markey came out draped in a trans pride flag and declared to raucous applause that "trans rights are human rights." The topic dominated the candidates' debates: in July, Markey said Moulton had "thrown trans kids under the bus" and noted that the Supreme Court's ruling greenlighting trans sports bans "took the same position that Congressman Moulton took last year," and by the August debate, Moulton was issuing a half-hearted mea culpa, saying he was "sorry if my comments hurt you.” Meanwhile, transgender people and LGBTQ+ organizations organized heavily to keep Markey in office, and those efforts succeeded.
There is good evidence that transgender issues were a major part of Markey's victory, too. In the final weeks of the campaign, a UMass Amherst/WCVB poll asked likely Democratic primary voters how a candidate who "expressed positions opposing transgender rights or policies" would fare with them. A whopping 67% said they would be less likely to support that candidate; only 11% said such positions would make their support more likely. Importantly, the poll's voter pool includes the unenrolled independent voters who can cast ballots in Massachusetts's semi-open Democratic primary, which should be a major lesson for Democrats elsewhere who believe running on anti-trans policies will win over the middle.
When Markey took the stage on Tuesday night to celebrate his victory, he made clear who he credited with helping him across the finish line. The very first person he put on stage was Tyler Hack, the transgender founder and executive director of the Christopher Street Project, the trans-led political organization that made his race its marquee endorsement, who introduced Markey to the crowd. Hack celebrated Markey's allyship in stark terms: "After the 2024 election, a lot of transgender people were terrified. And I remember thinking: Who is going to stay? When people decide we are too controversial, when defending us stops being expedient, who is going to stay? Ed Markey stayed. Senator, you stayed." When Markey took the microphone, he concurred, thanking "Tyler Hack and the Christopher Street Project" by name from the podium: "I am so proud of your historic work."
Update: It would appear trans flags have appeared outside of Moulton’s district office with a “for rent” sign. Curtesy of Jennifer G on Bluesky.

sources.text:
Photo: Sen. Ed Markey (Senate Democrats, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons)
Democrat Massachusetts Sen. Ed Markey defeated Democrat Massachusetts Rep. Seth Moulton Tuesday in a landslide, marking a rare win for the old-guard incumbents.
Young Democratic candidates have largely defeated older incumbents in 2026 primary elections. Eighty-year-old Markey defied that precedent by beating 47-year-old Moulton, who is more moderate than the incumbent.
Markey co-sponsored the Green New Deal, supported Medicare for All and received endorsements from independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, Democratic New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Democratic Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren and “Squad” member Democratic Massachusetts Rep. Ayanna Pressley. Further-left candidates have won several races and defeated incumbents throughout the 2026 cycle, including Democratic Colorado congressional candidate Melat Kiros, who defeated longtime incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette in July.
The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) is on pace to field its largest congressional delegation in its history. Young, college-educated voters have turned out in droves to support younger, more progressive candidates.
It is less common for older incumbents to defeat their younger opponents in recent Democratic primaries. Democratic Reps. Shri Thanedar of Michigan, John Larson of Connecticut and Adriano Espaillat of New York — who are all over the age of 70 — all lost their races to younger candidates.
“Democratic voters are hungry for a new generation of leaders who can credibly argue they’ll fight for change” Amanda Litman, founder of left-wing group Run For Something, told Axios.
Moulton ran as the moderate, receiving endorsements from Democratic New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, Democratic New York Rep. Pat Ryan and Democratic Rhode Island Rep. Seth Magaziner, according to his campaign website. He campaigned on affordability, outlined a plan for encounters with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and creating a public option for healthcare.
Markey supports allowing irreversible procedures for trans-identifying minors, abolishing ICE and implementing “universal healthcare,” according to his campaign website.
This is the second consecutive election cycle in which Markey prevailed against a younger challenger. In 2020, the then-74-year-old senator defeated then-39-year-old Rep. Joe Kennedy III — the nephew of now Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. —in the Democratic Senate primary.
Markey has held elected political office since 1973, when Richard Nixon was president — five years before Moulton was born. He served in the Massachusetts State House from that year to 1976, the U.S. House from 1976 to 2013 and the Senate since 2013.
Some older House Democrats faced pressure to drop out and ultimately did not run for reelection. These Democrats included Jerry Nadler of New York, Steve Cohen of Tennessee, Lloyd Doggett of Texas and Eleanor Holmes Norton. Cohen faced a primary challenge from 31-year-old Tennessee state Rep. Justin Pearson, and ultimately dropped out after Tennessee redrew his district’s lines.

Establishment Dems Win Again: 80-Year-Old Crank Lefty Fends Off 'Young' 47-Year-Old Challenger In Mass. Senate Primary
The party that has been stung over and over again by the gerontocracy and the diminishing returns that come with age — from Joe Biden to Dianne Feinstein to Eleanor Holmes Norton — was offered an off-ramp to another potential catastrophe within the establishment on Tuesday.
Surprise of surprises, it sped right on past.
In a race that was mostly seen as a litmus test on whether or not Democrats would keep electing officials to terms they couldn’t honestly say they could complete in full health and sound mind, 80-year-old Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts won the nomination for the Senate seat in a reliably Democratic state over 47-year-old U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton.
Yes, we’re now in an era where 47 represents “a new generation of leadership,” as Moulton put it. The last president from Massachusetts, you may recall, was just one year younger when he died, and he had already served as a representative and senator before assuming the presidency.
But according to The Washington Post, Massachusetts voters still think that Markey will be up to the task when he’s 86, overwhelmingly sending him back (yeah, there’s a Republican in the general election, but this is Massachusetts) by a 64.9 percent to 35.1 percent margin.
“Despite a rough year for establishment candidates, Markey led in polls throughout the race, in large part because he is viewed as more progressive in a state that skews leftward,” the outlet reported, noting that Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez had supported him.
Markey’s progressive bona fides, such as they exist, include loudly banging on about how the Democrats need to expand the Supreme Court because seats were “stolen” from them by those lousy Republicans. He’s promised to nuke the filibuster and basically put the entire population of Seattle on the high court if he gets the chance.
He also believes boys who identify as transgender should be able to play in girls’ sports, and Moulton doesn’t. In other words, he’s stuck in the summer of 2020, and probably always will be.
“Massachusetts needs a senator who stands up and fights back, a senator who never forgets who they are fighting for,” Markey said in his victory speech, according to the Associated Press.
“That has been the mission of my life, and it always will be.”
Realistically, outside of court packing, Markey is no longer a change agent and shows no signs of becoming one if given another six years in the upper chamber. He’s been in Congress since Gerald Ford was president and was handed John Kerry’s Senate seat when Kerry became Secretary of State under Obama. But, he insisted Tuesday, just because he lacks any sort of major accomplishment in the role doesn’t mean he’s not getting the little things done.
“Generational change isn’t about compromising, to do the small things better,” Markey told supporters. “It’s about fighting to do the big things best.”
Right. Like cable media hits, which Markey has become the undisputed champion of. Think Michael Avenatti, just over a longer period of time, with an elected office, and without any felony convictions or disbarments. But more of a crank:

When not on friendly territory like CNN or MS NOW, however, he looks a lot more like this rhetorical mess that’s definitely showing his age:

On my watch, the FCC is holding broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations. pic.twitter.com/2vQpwOcHmG

Here’s a man who, just in the 21st century alone, has been an election denier (he refused to vote to certify the 2004 Ohio results as a House member, thanks to the vague conspiracy theories that election machines manufactured by Diebold handed George W. Bush the state or whatever) and a supporter of convicting an impeached former president for denying election results:
Donald Trump is responsible for the coup that is unfolding at the Capitol. He is a fascist and a direct threat to our country.
— Ed Markey (@EdMarkey) January 6, 2021
Court packing is not going to happen anytime soon, and it likely won’t be happening with Markey leading the charge. What will happen is that we’ll end up with another Biden, another Feinstein, another Holmes Norton: Someone elected to do an exigent job for a constituency while being past that sad but inescapable point of diminishing returns that comes with age.
The only good thing that could be said about Tuesday’s result, I suppose, is that it couldn’t happen to a better state than the only one which cast its electoral votes for George McGovern in 1972.
If you’re too young to know who that is, just ask Ed Markey. That is, if he remembers.

Generational change candidates lose in MA. 3 takeaways from primary
- Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., defeated Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate.
- Rep. Stephen Lynch, D-Mass., fended off his primary challenge in lawyer Patrick Roath in the state's 8th Congressional District.
- Michael Minogue, a 59-year-old businessman and inventor, defeated Brian Shortsleeve, a former MBTA administrator, in the GOP primary for Massachusetts governor.
The message of generational change didn’t win last night in Massachusetts, as all of the incumbent federal Democratic lawmakers held off their primary challengers.
Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., defeated Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate. Rep. Stephen Lynch, D-Mass., fended off his primary challenge in lawyer Patrick Roath. And the three other representatives who faced similar challengers also won another term in office.
Still, that doesn’t mean an end for the movement. UMass Poll Director Tatishe Nteta said in an interview a few days before the primary that even if none of the change candidates got elected, the unusually high number of challenges proves many Democrats are unhappy with the current leadership and raises the question of whether the party will try to respond to that ferment.
He said he expects to see the same level of challengers, and maybe even better and well-funded ones, next election cycle.
“It's a bubbling cauldron, and not over exploding as of yet, of the need for movement by some members of Congress to cede to the next generation,” Nteta said. “The case for generational change is much more acute and much more powerful when individuals again continue to run for re-election into their early 80s.”
Here are three major takeaways from the Massachusetts primary last night.
Markey overcomes age-focused attacks to defeat Moulton
Markey handily defeated Moulton in the U.S. Senate primary, with the election called for the longtime senator less than 30 minutes after the close of polls.
Moulton had attacked Markey for his age, saying that it was time for a new generation of leaders. Markey is 80, while Moulton is 47. But polls before the primary suggested that voters cared more about Markey’s progressive policies and experience than his age, and the results Tuesday supported that.
This election marks the second time in as many cycles that Markey has defeated a much younger challenger. In 2020, he beat then Rep. Joe Kennedy.
But it doesn’t mean there isn’t an appetite for change. Instead, Markey may just have been more in step with the state’s Democratic electorate. Throughout the campaign, he stressed his progressive credentials, referencing the Green New Deal, touting endorsements from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and attacking Moulton for comments he made about transgender athletes.
“I think with Senator Markey, the challenger is not the correct challenger in terms of their characteristics to press on some of the weaknesses of Senator Markey. But you could imagine a more progressive challenger who has those bonafides, who's making a similar case, who is able to mobilize prominent Democrats in the state, then the argument for generational change, the argument about tenure in Congress, and the argument about age might have hit harder,” Nteta said. “This might not be an issue of the message. It might be an issue of the messenger.”
But as it stands, Markey is likely to serve his third full term in the U.S. Senate as the race is rated "Solid D" by the Cook Political Report. He will face Republican John Deaton in the November general election.
All House incumbents hold onto their seat
Of the state’s nine U.S. House members, four faced primary opponents who ran on messages of generational change this primary. All were able to hold on to their seat on Tuesday.
The unusually high number of primary challenges against incumbents in the Bay State follows a national trend. Around the country, Democrats running against a more experienced, usually older opponent, have been calling for change.
While many, including activist Darializa Avila Chevalier, 32, who beat five-term Rep. Adriano Espaillat, 71, in New York and former Hartford, Connecticut, Mayor Luke Bronin, 47, who beat 14-term Rep. John Larson, 78, won off that message, none of the candidates in Massachusetts were able to defeat their incumbents.
In the 1st District, which covers much of the western and central parts of Massachusetts, Rep. Richard Neal, 77, defeated teacher Jeromie Whalen, 39. Rep. Jake Auchincloss, 38, defeated Jason Poulos, a 40-year-old AI researcher, in the Democratic primary for the 4th Congressional District. In the 5th District, which includes suburbs north and west of Boston, House Minority Whip Rep. Katherine Clark, 63, beat Tarik Samman, a 27-year-old union organizer and Harvard Law School researcher, and Jonathan Paz, a 33-year-old former Waltham city councilor and immigrant rights organizer. In the 8th District, Rep. Stephen Lynch, 73, overcame lawyer Patrick Roath, 39. And in the 9th District, which encompasses Cape Cod and southern parts of the South Shore, Rep. Bill Keating, 73, triumphed over consultant Craig Swallow, 40.
Defeating incumbents is historically difficult: according to a 2016 review by Ballotpedia, House and Senate incumbents nationwide have been reelected at rates over 93% and 87% respectively. Incumbents benefit from name recognition and being able to point to accomplishments like bringing home federal funding for projects in their district.
Even though the incumbents won, Nteta said that just the number of challenges suggests that large chunks of the representatives’ constituencies are not happy with their leadership.
“The question is whether they're going to react to that or are they going to continue to do what they've done in the past,” Nteta said.
All of the incumbents are now almost certain to win another term in Congress in the deep blue state.
Minogue likely faces uphill battle against Healey in MA gov race
One non-generational change-related race on the ballot Tuesday was the Republican primary for Massachusetts governor.
Here, Michael Minogue, a 59-year-old businessman and inventor, defeated Brian Shortsleeve, a former MBTA administrator. He will face incumbent Gov. Maura Healey, who was uncontested in the Democratic primary, in the November election.
Minogue supports immigration enforcement and cutting taxes, and says he would cancel “unfunded mandates” like the MBTA Communities Act, which requires towns with commuter rail lines to build a certain amount of housing near the transportation. He is also anti-abortion, although he has said he would uphold the Massachusetts law if elected.
Minogue likely has a challenge ahead of him. The Massachusetts governor race is rated “Solid D” by the Cook Political Report, and two polls released before the primary showed Healey handily beating Minogue in a hypothetical matchup: 54% to 30% in a University of New Hampshire Survey Center poll, and 53% to 33% in a UMass Poll.
“Since Charlie Baker left the governor’s office, Massachusetts Republicans have been searching for a candidate capable of defeating Democratic Governor Maura Healey,” UMass Poll Director Tatishe Nteta said in a press release. “But our findings suggest that the Republican nominee will face a steep uphill climb this fall.”
Nteta said in an interview before the primary that the Republican winner would have an opportunity to criticize Healey on issues like cost of living, affordability and housing, which are all important to voters. However, it might be a hard thing for Minogue to argue, he said, as a multi-millionaire who largely self-funded his campaign.
Plus, Healey is a fairly popular incumbent: in both polls, her approval rating was above 50%. It’s also a progressive state, and the midterm elections are likely to revolve around what’s going on at the White House, Nteta said, which benefits Democrats.

sources.news_title: Seth Moulton’s anti-trans shape-shifting ends in a humiliating blowout in Massachusetts
sources.text:
Rep. Seth Moulton went looking for a promotion and found the exit.
Massachusetts Democrats overwhelmingly rejected the congressman’s bid for U.S. Senate on Tuesday, renominating Sen. Ed Markey after a campaign that turned Moulton’s attacks on transgender athletes into a test of whether a Democrat could betray part of the party’s coalition and call it courage.
It was not close.
Markey received 556,865 votes, or 64.88 percent, compared with Moulton’s 301,372 votes, or 35.12 percent, according to Decision Desk HQ. With 91 percent of the estimated vote reported Wednesday morning, Markey led by 255,493 votes — a nearly 30-point demolition.
Related: Seth Moulton’s anti-trans rhetoric comes back to haunt him in Senate debate with Ed Markey
Moulton, 47, had built his campaign around the proposition that Markey, 80, represented a Democratic Party too old and too comfortable to meet the moment. But the novelty of a politician is not the same as the novelty of their politics. In perhaps the race’s sharpest contrast, the older candidate ran unapologetically in defense of transgender people. The younger one spent much of the campaign explaining why he had not.
“Tonight, anti-trans politics lost,” Tyler Hack, executive director of the Christopher Street Project, said after Markey’s victory. “Massachusetts rejected the idea that attacking transgender people is a shortcut to political power.”
Moulton’s transformation began after Donald Trump won the 2024 presidential election. The congressman had compiled a long record of supporting LGBTQ+ legislation. Then, as some Democrats searched for a conveniently powerless constituency to blame, Moulton told The New York Times that he did not want his daughters “getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete.”
Related: Pro-trans rival draws cheers after Rep. Seth Moulton booed at Boston No Kings rally
The remark borrowed the right’s preferred fiction: that transgender girls are not girls but dangerous male bodies invading spaces where they do not belong. Moulton presented his willingness to repeat that framing as evidence that he was prepared to have difficult conversations other Democrats supposedly feared.
In a subsequent exclusive interview with The Advocate, Moulton insisted that his intentions were protective. Republicans, he said, had run “hateful but effective ads,” and Democrats risked surrendering the debate if they refused to engage.
Yet Moulton’s legislative record never fit neatly with his rhetoric. He voted against a Republican bill barring transgender students from girls’ and women’s sports. He supported the Equality Act and the Transgender Bill of Rights. He also helped lead a bipartisan effort to save the LGBTQ+ youth service within the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.
Moulton wanted voters to view those positions as compatible with his attacks on transgender athletes. Many transgender people instead saw an ally looking for the exit the moment allyship appeared politically costly.
The contradiction followed him into the Senate campaign. At Boston’s No Kings rally in October 2025, Moulton was met with boos. Markey appeared draped in a transgender Pride flag and drew loud applause when he declared that “trans rights are human rights.”
By an August debate, Moulton was trying to shape-shift again.
“I deeply recognize your trauma, and I’m sorry if my comments hurt you,” he said, delivering a qualified apology before reciting his LGBTQ+ credentials. Markey replied that Moulton had taken Trump’s playbook and thrown transgender children “under the political bus.” The exchange dragged the comments Moulton wanted to contextualize back into the center of the race.
The Associated Press identified transgender rights as perhaps the campaign’s defining issue. Moulton also attacked Markey’s age, knowledge of artificial intelligence and decades in Washington. But he could never establish that changing generations required abandoning progressive principles — or that a politician offering older prejudices in a younger package constituted progress.
Related: Democrat Seth Moulton defends comments on trans athletes amid backlash (exclusive)
U.S. Rep. Ayanna Pressley, one of Markey’s most prominent surrogates, said Massachusetts had selected a senator who “gives a damn” and “has never wavered in his commitment to workers and families.”
“With Trump and Republicans moving with malice and enacting widespread harm, Massachusetts sent a clear message: We want Democrats who will defend our communities and never back down,” Pressley said in a statement.
The National Federation of Stonewall Democrats issued a similar warning to candidates who view LGBTQ+ rights as negotiable. “Our safety and our dignity are not bargaining chips, and any candidate who treats them that way should expect to lose our support,” federation President Jeremy Comeau said in a statement. “Candidates who stand up for trans kids and defend the rights of LGBTQ+ Americans can win, and win decisively.”
Human Rights Campaign President Kelley Robinson pointed to Markey’s consistency.
“He knows why equality matters,” Robinson said in a statement from HRC’s political action committee. “He’s stood with us no matter what.”
At Markey’s victory celebration, Hack argued that the result carried a lesson beyond Massachusetts.
“We don’t accept a younger politician with older politics,” Hack said. “Equality cannot be something Democrats believe in only when it is easy. Civil rights cannot depend on a focus group.”
Moulton conceded Tuesday night and pledged to support Markey against Republican John Deaton in November. “We didn’t achieve our goal tonight, but I am confident others will be inspired to buck the system when they’re told to wait their turn,” he told supporters.
Moulton gave up his House seat to pursue the Senate, meaning his failed bid is also expected to end his congressional career in January.

sources.news_title: Taking Stock of the Midterms, Three Months Out
sources.text:
Where Are We Two Months Out From the Election?
Following last night’s election in Massachusetts — which, in the most closely-watched race, saw Democratic Sen. Ed Markey demolish a primary challenge from the much younger Rep. Seth Moulton — we’re coming to the end of primary season and turning to the general election. New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Delaware still need to hold their nominating contests, which will happen over the next two weeks.
So, I wanted to take today to assess what kind of general election we’re likely to see, and examine some of the factors likely to shape it.
Hanging over all of it, of course, are Trump’s schemes to meddle in the results. His allied, right-wing influencers are, daily, cheering him on, pushing him to go further.
He’s already done quite a bit.
According to a postal service whistleblower who spoke to the Senate, that agency, scrambling to comply with Trump’s executive order on mail-in voting, is in the midst of implementing a brand new system for sending ballots to voters. “Catastrophic failure would be a feature rather than a bug,” the whistleblower’s lawyers wrote of this “slapdash” effort.
It will require state election officials to feed into two USPS systems lists of voters which must match up exactly. Each ballot will then get a bar code, which will then be matched with the lists and, again, must align exactly. The system as described creates huge opportunity for human and technical error — and, the whistleblower warned, an error on a single ballot could lead to a whole tranche being rejected. “As presently designed, if even one bar code on one single ballot in a bulk-mailing of 10,000 ballots fails to properly scan during the verification process, the entire batch is rejected and sent back to the state – effectively stopping the ballots from being mailed to voters,” the whistleblower complaint reads.
I asked the postal service about these claims, and a spokesperson did not contest them, instead saying that the agency would provide state officials “who voluntarily wish to familiarize themselves with the platform” with “tools, presentations, and other resources.”
It will be up to the Supreme Court whether this program moves forward. If it does, it stands to have a considerable impact on who votes, and how they do it.
Trump and his allies may well threaten the election in other ways, too. As I wrote yesterday, a federal law enforcement agency within Immigrations and Customs Enforcement, Homeland Security Investigations, is surging resources to root out “voter fraud,” seemingly seeking to substantiate the baseless Republican talking point that noncitizens are voting en masse. (To be clear, there is absolutely no evidence this is happening; each state has systems in place to match ballots to registered voters, and noncitizens are barred by law from registering to vote in federal elections. The extremely infrequent exceptions to this — such as a data error in New Jersey that erroneously allowed noncitizens to register, which was made public by the state — did not impact the outcome of any election.)
Worries persist that Trump administration officials will order ICE to the polls, declare a national emergency to meddle with the election outcome, or try to prevent Democrats from being seated when the next Congress is sworn in on January 3. Laws bar each of these things from happening, but the Stop the Steal campaign of 2020 and early 2021, culminating in but not ending with Jan. 6, teaches us not to underestimate how far Trump may go to create and exploit chaos, and administration officials avoid every chance they get to disabuse the public of its concerns about each of these scenarios.
Turning away from Trump and toward the electoral map, things look pretty good for Democrats (though, as Off Message’s Brian Beutler writes and I agree, the self-imposed, left-of-center, national media struggle session around streamer Hasan Piker is doing no one any favors; especially when one of the top Republican Senate candidates is seemingly surrounded by white nationalists and antisemites). “Republicans should brace themselves: The three most plausible outcomes are that it will be bad, really bad, or truly horrible,” Charlie Cook of Cook Political Report wrote yesterday.
On the other hand, theres the possibility our sense of things right now is overly favorable to Democrats — there’s the spectre of a polling error that has reared its head in recent elections, where Democrats come out of the summer with inflated numbers that draw closer to reality as Election Day approaches. There’s really no good way I’ve read about to figure out if that’s happening again.
There’s still room for a surprise, too, beyond Trump’s almost-inevitable effort to meddle. Though we’ve been told we’re on the cusp of a recession for years, the bond market is looking very ominous.
So anyway, those are the factors I — and, to some extent, TPM — have in mind as we look toward Election Day. It is my job to think and talk about this all day, but I’m just one person. You can email me at john@talkingpointsmemo.com, or, if you’re receiving this by email, simply hit reply. Let me know what you’re paying attention to.
A New Take on the 2026 Dynamic
The headline race in Massachusetts was a little unusual — an 80-year-old progressive incumbent versus a more moderate, younger challenger who had drawn the party base’s ire with his on again-off again criticism of trans athletes in sports. In races across the country this year we’ve seen younger, often more progressive challengers oust veteran incumbents, part of a push among the base for generational change. It seems that the Massachusetts voters who chose Markey over Moulton found that, in this case, the older man would best bring the fight to Trump
Here are some other takeaways from the primary.
- Two other older guys held on — Reps. Stephen Lynch and Richard Neal won the nomination against younger challengers.
- Dan Koh, a veteran of the Biden administration, won against a more progressive opponent, Tram Nguyen.
- This wasn’t on the ballot last night, but it will be in November: Massachusetts is looking to move to a top-two primary system. “It’s a terrible idea!” writes political scientist Jonathan Bernstein. “The whole idea behind it is to destroy the ability of political parties to nominate candidates as they see fit, which is pretty much the basis for party health.” After watching the stressful spectacle in California earlier this year, I find that argument convincing!
Tabs
- New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Governor Kathy Hochul said Tuesday that Trump reneged on a promise to restore $187 million in counterterrorism funding his administration had withheld. The city and state got $100 million, but is still awaiting the rest, officials said. “Release the $87 million you owe us. Because if you don’t release the counterterrorism funding, you’re betraying every family that lost someone on 9/11,” Hochul said at a press conference, per Politico.
- The Atlantic tracked down the family whose child’s death formed the basis of a political fight over measles in Pennsylvania. It’s a moving piece about an Amish family that has no idea about the political battle their child’s death set off, or even who the main participants — HHS Secretary RFK Jr. and Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro — are.
Man of the Hour
It’s Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, continuing to entertain the theoretical possibility there might be valid reasons to send ICE officers to the polls this November. (He describes a far-fetched scenario in which a noncitizen individual whom ICE is actively pursuing basically flees into a polling place, leaving officers with no choice but to follow him in: “The only reason why we would be at polling places is if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down.”)
Are We at War?
New strikes on Iran — perhaps this is an attempt to “mow the lawn” — amid a global bond selloff that is fueled, in part, by the economic effects of the war. It comes as the Pentagon has completely cut off the press. “Frankly, they don’t even think they owe the public any information,” a reporter who works for a trade publication told the Columbia Journalism Review. “They’re hiding behind this idea that they can just say, ‘It’s a war, so we don’t have to communicate with you.’ This is often what we hear from public affairs officers.”
Correction: This post originally said we are three, not two months out from the election. How embarrassing. We are two months out.
Math is not my strong point, but I count 2 months not 3 until November.
I sense a possible disconnect in the way the Postal Service is handling this ballot issue. I don’t know about other states, but in Ohio, the state does not send out the mail-in ballots, the counties do. That would create 88 ways to screw up ballot distribution in just one state.
Markwayne Mullin is giving stupidity a bad name.
I’m from Massachusetts and voted for Markey. As far as I’m concerned Moulton is Republican lite. I haven’t trusted him since he was part of the attempted coup to oust Nancey Pelosi.
Not certain how I feel about the top two primary. I like the idea of removing the influence of parties from the electoral process. But I see this as an attempt by republicans to give themselves a chance to win seats in a state that is majorly democratic. Almost a reverse gerrymander.
If you don’t agree, please try to change my mind.

sources.news_title: Markey’s victory caps strong night for Massachusetts progressives
sources.text:
Markey’s victory caps strong night for Massachusetts progressives
The longtime senator easily fended off a generational challenge from Rep. Seth Moulton, with Markey taking home nearly two-thirds of the primary vote
(Craig F. Walker/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)
Ideological progressivism and incumbency proved to be more potent advantages than an argument for generational change in the Massachusetts Senate primary, where Sen. Ed Markey (D-MA) easily dispatched a challenge from more-moderate Rep. Seth Moulton (D-MA), who nonetheless swung leftward during the primary campaign.
Markey, a lifelong politician first elected to Congress in 1976, locked down support from the state’s leading progressives, including Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) and Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-MA) — and won backing from the stars of socialist wing of the party, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY).
That progressive show of support was more than enough to inoculate Markey over questions Moulton raised about the 80-year-old congressman’s age — the challenger’s most frequent line of attack that ended up falling flat. Markey won a sweeping victory, tallying nearly two-thirds (65%) of the Democratic vote and winning the vast majority of towns and cities in the state.
Moulton, despite holding a largely pro-Israel record during his time in Congress, made a show of attacking the pro-Israel advocacy group AIPAC in one of his Senate campaign’s first moves — a strategy that earned him enmity from some of his former moderate allies and bought him little goodwill from the progressive wing of the party. (Moulton also unsuccessfully sought AIPAC’s support before turning on the organization.)
The Democratic Party’s turn to the left was apparent in the state’s congressional primary results as well. All the Democratic incumbents prevailed, but two veteran politicians received scares from their left flank.
Rep. Richard Neal (D-MA), the ranking Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, survived a challenge from progressive Jeromie Whalen, a high school teacher who made cutting aid to Israel a major plank in his campaign platform. But Neal’s margin — winning by only seven points — was remarkably narrow for a longtime incumbent and a sign of growing left-wing energy in the state.
Meanwhile, Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-MA), a pro-union moderate Democrat, defeated Patrick Roath, a voting rights advocate who ran on a progressive platform calling for generational change and embracing Medicare for All. With most precincts reporting, Lynch prevailed with 57% of the vote.
Rep. Jake Auchincloss (D-MA), a moderate Democrat who has become more critical of Israel in recent months, comfortably prevailed against a long-shot challenger, winning 73% of the primary vote.
And in the open seat to succeed Moulton, former Biden administration official Dan Koh comfortably outdistanced state Rep. Tram Nguyen, who was endorsed by the progressive Pressley.

sources.news_title: 80-Year-Old Sen. Ed Markey Holds Off Younger Challenger in Democratic Primary
sources.text:
Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts won the Democratic primary race for his seat on Tuesday, fending off a challenge from the decades-younger Rep. Seth Moulton as he seeks another six-year term in the upper chamber.
Running on a progressive platform, Markey adds to a series of primary wins including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, suggesting an appetite among Democratic primary voters for a shift away from the center.
Read More: Congress Is Headed for a Massive Turnover
Moulton’s campaign focused largely on affordable housing and health care. His efforts to position himself as a fresh voice in politics ultimately failed against Markey’s decades of experience.
With around 96% of the ballots counted early Wednesday, Markey had 64.9% of the vote to Moulton's 35.1%.
“Massachusetts needs a Senator who stands up and fights back, a Senator who never forgets who they are fighting for,” Markey told the crowd during his victory speech. “That has been the mission of my life, and it always will be.”
A ‘generational showdown’
Tuesday’s primary was considered by many to be a “generational showdown” between Markey, 80, and Moulton, 47.
During the campaign, Moulton contended that it was time for change in the state's political representation.
“Massachusetts has a choice: settle for the status quo, or demand better,” he wrote in a social media post Tuesday.
The young moderate rose in the polls earlier this year, narrowing the gap between himself and the two-term incumbent. But in the month or so leading up to Tuesday’s primary, polls showed that Markey had regained ground and was holding a comfortable double-digit lead.
This isn’t the first time Markey, who served in the House for nearly 37 years before winning a seat in the Senate in 2013, has held off a younger primary challenger. In his last reelection bid, the then-74-year-old Senator defeated then-Rep. Joseph Kennedy III, who is 34 years his junior, to advance to the November ballot.
Progressives notch another primary victory
Markey has built up a long progressive record over his years in Congress, co-sponsoring the Green New Deal alongside Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and championing left-wing positions on an array of issues. And he made that record—as well as his extensive experience—a focus of his campaign. Markey argued during the primary that Moulton’s stances on various issues don't align with those of their constituents in deep-blue Massachusetts, saying that “there’s only one progressive in this race” and that “we don’t just need a democratic majority in the Senate. We need a progressive majority.”
“It’s not about your age, it’s about the age of your ideas. And I am the youngest guy in this race when it comes to ideas,” Markey told POLITICO. “Democrats want a victory this November.
