Abandoning Core Beliefs Fails To Save Seth Moulton From Humiliating Loss
sources.text:
So much for Seth.
Rep. Seth Moulton's bid for U.S. Senate in Massachusetts ended Tuesday in an inglorious defeat in the Democratic primary at the hands of the incumbent, Senator Ed Markey, 80.
At 10 and a half months, Moulton's Senate bid lasted longer than his 2020 presidential campaign, which expired in August 2019 after 4 months. He managed to win the endorsement of the Boston Globe, the state's largest newspaper. But Moulton, a 47-year-old ex-Marine with three degrees from Harvard, didn't win enough votes in the primary to proceed, leaving his Senate race with the same outcome as his presidential campaign: a loss. With 96 percent of the vote in, he was trailing by 30 points.
The significance goes beyond Moulton's political career. It points to the difficulty of dislodging an incumbent senator—news that will come as no solace to John Cornyn, Republican of Texas, but that may help reassure Susan Collins, Republican of Maine. It points to the tenuous road for moderate candidates in Democratic primary politics. Most of all, though, it is a demonstration that totally abandoning whatever principles you had, or were pretending to have, is no recipe for victory.
Malleability is sometimes counted as a political plus, as in the hoary joke about the politician who says, "those are my principles, and if you don't like them… well, I have others." But Moulton managed to take that approach so far in his 2026 campaign—running away from any of his own moderate positions that might conceivably differentiate him from Markey—that the overall effect was less self-deprecating than it was abjectly pathetic. Instead of pragmatic, Moulton seemed inauthentic.
Among the areas where Moulton flip-flopped:
Business, taxes, and class warfare. One of his three degrees from Harvard is an MBA, and Moulton kicked off his presidential campaign in 2019 by pointedly declaring, "I'm not a socialist." He denounced tax increases on the rich as "class warfare." As a member of Congress, he has not signed on as a cosponsor to two pieces of tax-the-rich legislation.
Yet as a Senate candidate, he's promising a $3.5 trillion tax increase based on "a national wealth tax on mega-millionaires."
Israel. Moulton started out pro-Israel. On October 7, 2023, he said, "I stand firmly with Israel and unequivocally affirm its right to defend itself and its people." He called the Harvard student organization letter holding Israel "entirely responsible" for the violence "intellectually weak and morally repugnant," declaring, "I cannot recall a moment when I've been more embarrassed by my alma mater." In December 2023, he criticized Harvard's then-president, Claudine Gay: "Moral leadership rarely comes in the form of defensive explanations. People are 'confused' because you refused to unequivocally state that advocating genocide has no place in the Harvard community. ... Wouldn't it have been powerful to see university leaders join together in committing to combat the shocking rise of antisemitism in America, rather than uniting to avoid answering a simple question."
Yet Moulton kicked off his Senate campaign with an attack on the main pro-Israel lobby, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, performatively refusing to accept donations from it. He also pledged to return all the money he had accepted from AIPAC, which he failed to do. Instead, he returned the funds he'd received from the group in the 2026 cycle.
Cultural issues. In a November 2024 post-election interview with the New York Times, Moulton suggested that the Democrats could benefit from being less doctrinaire on the issue of men in women's sports: "I have two little girls, I don't want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete, but as a Democrat I'm supposed to be afraid to say that." The remarks came after Trump soared to victory over Kamala Harris in part on the basis of a television commercial highlighting Harris's response to a 2019 ACLU questionnaire in which she said she supported taxpayer-funded sex-change operations for illegal aliens. "Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you," the ad said.
Yet in the Senate campaign, Moulton apologized for those comments. "To the trans community, feeling the weight and the pain of the Trump administration policies, I deeply recognize your trauma, and I'm sorry if my comments hurt you. That was not my intention," Moulton said during an August 3, 2026 debate. "I'm a proud sponsor of the transgender bill of rights, a proud repeat cosponsor of the Equality Act, and I have a 100 percent record with the Human Rights Campaign. If you're in the trans community, or you're a trans kid feeling the weight of the Trump administration and the Supreme Court, you matter, you're valued, and I will always have your back."
The cumulative effect of it all was to leave Massachusetts voters confused about what Moulton stood for other than his own ambition for higher office. The evolutions seemed awfully convenient for appealing to the left-leaning Massachusetts Democratic primary electorate, but they wound up turning off voters by appearing calculated rather than conviction-based. Maybe Moulton will be considered for the role of Secretary of Veterans Affairs in the next Democratic administration, or some transportation-related job—he's a high-speed rail enthusiast. Until then perhaps he will seek employment in the private sector, equipped with the painfully earned newfound knowledge that the public—even a segment of it as skewed as the Massachusetts Democratic primary electorate—can easily detect a phony.

Massachusetts primary results: Key takeaways
sources.text:
Ed Markey wins: Key takeaways from Massachusetts primary election results
Markey secures the Democratic nomination as Massachusetts voters back several of the state’s long-serving lawmakers.
Veteran Democrats defeated younger challengers in Massachusetts’s primary elections on Tuesday, with Senator Ed Markey beating Representative Seth Moulton for the Democratic nomination.
Long-serving representatives Stephen Lynch and Richard Neal also won their races.
Recommended Stories
list of 1 itemend of list
Here are five key takeaways from the Massachusetts primary election results.
Veteran Democrats survive challenges from younger rivals
Several of Massachusetts’s longest-serving Democrats survived challenges in Tuesday’s primaries.
Senator Ed Markey, 80, defeated 47-year-old Representative Seth Moulton to secure the Democratic nomination.
Similar challenges also failed in the House. Representative Stephen Lynch, 71, who has held his seat since 2001, defeated 39-year-old progressive lawyer Patrick Roath in the 8th Congressional District.
In the 1st District, 77-year-old Representative Richard Neal, first elected to Congress in 1988, defeated 39-year-old public school teacher Jeromie Whalen.
All three will now advance to November, with Democrats heavily favoured in Massachusetts.
Markey wins the progressive argument despite his age
Moulton campaigned on the need for a new generation of political leadership, but Markey’s age did not appear to work against him.
Markey, 33 years older than Moulton, ran as the more progressive candidate, with backing from prominent figures on the Democratic left, including Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and independent Senator Bernie Sanders.
Markey also had the backing of Senator Elizabeth Warren and other members of the state’s congressional delegation, while no member of the delegation endorsed Moulton.
Moulton, a Marine veteran who ran as the more moderate alternative, instead received support from groups including VoteVets and New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill.
Markey also repeatedly attacked Moulton over his comments questioning transgender girls’ participation in girls’ sports. Moulton later apologised and said he supported the transgender community, but Markey continued to raise the issue during the campaign.
“If you’re in the trans community or you’re a trans kid feeling the weight of the Trump administration and the Supreme Court, you matter,” Moulton said during an August debate. “You’re valued, and I will always have your back.”
However, the opposite dynamic played out in the 8th District, where the younger Roath — unsuccessfully — challenged Lynch from the left.
The results showed that age and ideology did not necessarily go hand in hand in Massachusetts.
“Generational change isn’t about compromising, to do the small things better,” Markey said Tuesday. “It’s about fighting to do the big things best.”
In a concession speech, Moulton said he would now support Markey.
“Challenging the establishment and calling for a new generation of leadership isn’t easy. But it is necessary,” Moulton told supporters. “We started conversations that needed to happen.”
Progressive challengers make gains but fall short
While younger challengers failed to defeat the state’s veteran Democrats, some still mounted competitive campaigns.
Roath raised about $1.3m compared with roughly $910,000 for Lynch, despite taking on a congressman who has represented the area for more than two decades.
He also significantly narrowed the gap during the campaign. Lynch led Roath by 26 points in a February poll, but by the final stretch of the campaign, his lead had narrowed to seven points.
But Roath ultimately fell short against Lynch.
Whalen also challenged Neal from the left in the 1st District, campaigning on progressive policies including Medicare for All, but fell short against the veteran congressman.
Massachusetts bucks the national trend
The Massachusetts results differed from several Democratic primaries elsewhere in the country, where younger progressive candidates have defeated long-serving politicians.
In Connecticut last month, former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin defeated Representative John Larson, 78, who had served in Congress for nearly three decades.
In June, 29-year-old Democratic socialist Melat Kiros defeated Representative Diana DeGette, who had represented her Colorado district for nearly 30 years.
That came a week after two Democratic members of Congress were defeated by left-wing challengers in New York, including five-term Representative Adriano Espaillat.
In Massachusetts, all three major challenges to long-serving lawmakers failed.
But the results were not necessarily a rejection of progressive politics. Markey himself ran from the party’s progressive wing, while Lynch and Neal faced younger candidates running to their left.
Instead, the common factor was the strength of long-serving politicians, regardless of whether their challengers came from the centre or the left.
Biden-backed Dan Koh wins primary for open House seat
Former Biden White House aide Koh won the Democratic primary for Massachusetts’s 6th Congressional District, the seat being vacated by Seth Moulton as he ran for Senate.
Koh stood out in the five-way race for openly embracing the former Biden administration. He was endorsed by former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris, as well as former Labor Secretary and Boston Mayor Marty Walsh.
Koh will now head into November as the favourite to win the heavily Democratic district.
Democratic primaries may have decided the races
In heavily Democratic Massachusetts, the primaries may prove to be the biggest electoral hurdle, with Democratic winners heavily favoured to prevail in November’s general election.
Markey will face Republican John Deaton, who ran unopposed in his primary on Tuesday. Deaton previously ran for the Senate against Elizabeth Warren in 2024, losing by about 20 percentage points.
The Democratic nominees in several House districts will also head into November as heavy favourites, meaning Tuesday’s results could in effect determine much of the state’s congressional delegation for the next term.

That situation involves Democratic candidates “running for the hills about AIPAC and treating it as a boogeyman,” added Robbins, who began organizing pro-Israel rallies in 2012, while chairing the New England Board of the Anti-Defamation League.

On Tuesday night, however, neither candidate referred directly to AIPAC. Moulton spoke only briefly, while Markey primarily focused on domestic issues but did quickly mention the Middle East.
“We need to end the war in Iran, and stop the bombing in Gaza,” Markey said. “We need to slash the Pentagon budget.”
The senator stressed the need to protect the LGBTQ+ community and to prioritize affordability goals, such as achieving “a future with no copays, no surprise bills, no premiums, no deductibles, a future with Medicare for all.”

sources.news_title: Markey leads incumbent sweep in Massachusetts
sources.text:
The News
Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., decisively won his primary on Tuesday, defeating Rep. Seth Moulton on a bad night for insurgent Democratic candidates.
Markey, who turned 80 this summer, defeated Moulton across the state, losing to the 47-year-old only in parts of Moulton’s northeast congressional district.
“Challenging the establishment and calling for a new generation of leadership isn’t easy, but it is necessary,” Moulton told supporters early in the night.
The Markey-Moulton race pitted an aging progressive against a younger Democrat with some more moderate views. It never settled into the generational change election that Moulton craved, as progressives and LGBTQ rights groups rallied behind the senator.
But no challenger to the all-Democratic Massachusetts delegation won on Tuesday. Two long-serving House members, Rep. Stephen Lynch and Rep. Richard Neal, held off younger primary opponents — both of whom ran to their left, portraying them as ineffective and compromised by campaign money.
In Moulton’s own district, former White House staffer Dan Koh won the nomination to succeed him, after running the only campaign ads this cycle that featured endorsements from Joe Biden and Kamala Harris.
In this article:
David’s view
Plenty went into Markey’s victory over a much younger opponent. Moulton didn’t have the goodwill or local Democratic support of Rep. Joe Kennedy III, who challenged Markey in 2020. He ran a more negative campaign than Kennedy had, with one attack that definitely backfired — pointing to mentions of the senator in “the Epstein files,” which suggested no wrongdoing by Markey at all.
But a defining issue in this race was transgender rights, and specifically the right of transgender girls to play girls’ sports. The week that Democrats lost the 2024 election, Moulton told The New York Times that his party was too afraid to “offend anyone” and had handed Republicans too many issues: “I have two little girls, I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete.”
Moulton’s district had rejected Donald Trump by 21 points, and progressives there denounced him for “scapegoating” trans people. For a few weeks, Moulton embraced the controversy he’d stirred, calling for a debate inside his party that could help it develop a position on a tricky issue.
Then he stopped. In 2025, as the new administration and friendly courts wiped out the Biden administration’s pro-trans policies, Moulton basically quit talking about the issue. Days after Moulton launched his challenge to Markey, the senator spoke at Boston’s No Kings rally with a pink, white, and blue trans flag draped around his shoulders.
By the summer, when Moulton had gained some ground against Markey, the congressman had co-sponsored Markey’s Transgender Bill of Rights resolution, which would have called on Congress to ban discrimination based on gender identity, including in school sports.
When I asked Moulton what his position was now, he said that “my 5-year-old who plays on the co-ed soccer team” could obviously play against trans girls, and “by the way, that was going to be outlawed by some of the Republicans’ extremist, hateful legislation.”
“We also need to have a conversation about what those rules should be,” he continued. “And I don’t know what the right answer is.”
By the end of the primary, Moulton had apologized for his November 2024 remarks — and Markey’s steadfast support for trans rights was part of his re-election argument. He was the bold progressive on the right side of history, and his opponent blew with the wind.
“My opponent threw trans kids under the bus after the 2024 election, blaming them for our losing of the election,” Markey said in his final debate with Moulton. “I, on the other hand — I introduced the Trans Bill of Rights so that all of the constitutional protections for every other American [are] extended to the trans community.”
And on Saturday, at a rally in Dorchester with Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and other high-profile endorsers, Markey gave the stage to Tyler Hack, the founder of the trans rights group the Christopher Street Project, who said that the election would be a referendum on whether people like her had a party to protect them.
“Every politician wondering whether abandoning trans people is good politics is watching,” Hack said. “And every trans kid who has spent the last two years watching adults debate whether they deserve healthcare, whether they deserve to play sports, whether they deserve to exist openly in this country and to grow old — they are watching, too.”
Markey and his allies won the argument in Massachusetts. The idea that the state is so reliably progressive, and needs to remain a bulwark against conservative federal politics, ran through the primary.
And while Markey campaigned, the Democratic nominees for governor in three Trump-won states — Ohio, Iowa, and Nevada — all said that they favored barring trans athletes from women’s and girls sports.
When Boston declared itself a “sanctuary city for transgender and LGBTQIA2s+” people, those were the kind of places they expected people to be fleeing. Moulton’s call for a debate on the question became, in Markey’s hands, a warning that he was too weak to fight when it mattered.
“I think across elections, voters are demonstrating that they want Democrats that are fighting for their principles,” Rep. Sarah McBride, the first and only transgender member of Congress, told me on Tuesday. “They can be pragmatic in how they do that, but they want Democrats who are fighting for their principles.”
Room for Disagreement
Markey’s win was disappointing to the small faction of Democrats who think the party must moderate its transgender rights positions.
“Rep. Moulton absolutely did the right thing in November 2024, saying that Dems across the board, elected and rank and file, need to have open and honest conversations,” said Kara Dansky, a member of the board of directors at Democrats for an Informed Approach to Gender, a group opposed to “gender ideology.”
“He never should have backtracked,” she said. “True-blue Massachusetts does not reflect the whole country. Voters across the spectrum, including rank and file Democrats, support female-only sports.”
Notable
- Markey sat for a few interviews as the campaign ended, telling Reid J. Epstein of The New York Times that “trans athletes should be able to play. That reflects Massachusetts and who we are.”
- In the 19th, Amanda Becker reported on the fight that broke out among Ohio Democrats after their nominee for governor backed the state’s current policy on excluding trans athletes.

sources.news_title: Sen. Ed Markey, 80, wins Mass. Democratic primary over Seth Moulton
sources.text:
U.S. Sen. Ed Markey secured the Democratic nomination in Massachusetts’ Senate primary for his reelection bid Tuesday, once again fending off a push for generational change as he seeks a third term.
Markey, 80, defeated U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton, 47, who argued that it was time to do away with the “status quo.”
Markey successfully pointed to Moulton’s more moderate positions to argue that it was Moulton — not the older incumbent — who was out of touch with the state’s voters.
Markey had boasted about his 2022 climate bill and called for an end to the war in Iran to bring down energy costs. He also sharply criticized Moulton for opposing “Medicare for All” — though Moulton called for universal healthcare.
Story continues below Trending Shorts
“He has a backwards-looking political agenda,” Markey said.
In heavily Democratic Massachusetts, the primary is considered the most critical election hurdle, and the winner is expected to prevail in the general election in November.
Markey has been a fixture in Massachusetts politics since the 1970s, prompting Moulton to make his “status quo” arguments on the campaign trail and to question Markey’s accomplishments during his lengthy time in office.
In a concession speech, Moulton said he would now support Markey.
“Challenging the establishment and calling for a new generation of leadership isn’t easy. But it is necessary,” Moulton told supporters. “We started conversations that needed to happen.”
“We didn’t achieve our goal tonight, but I am confident others will be inspired to buck the system when they’re told to wait their turn,” he added.
The Senate race was not the only generational challenge for Democrats on Tuesday’s ballot. A similar dynamic played out in the 8th Congressional District, where Patrick Roath hoped to oust longtime incumbent Rep. Stephen Lynch, and in the 1st Congressional District of western Massachusetts, where progressive public school teacher Jeromie Whalen faced against Rep. Richard Neal.
Moulton’s comments on transgender children were an issue
During the campaign Markey repeatedly pointed out that Moulton, in 2024, raised eyebrows among some in the party for saying he did not want his daughters playing sports against transgender girls.
Critics said he was echoing President Donald Trump’s talking points against allowing transgender athletes in girls’ and women’s sports.
Moulton later apologized for his remarks, saying it was not his intention to hurt the transgender community and stressing his support for other transgender rights bills.
“If you’re in the trans community or you’re a trans kid feeling the weight of the Trump administration and the Supreme Court, you matter,” Moulton said during an August debate. “You’re valued, and I will always have your back.”
Moulton, who enlisted in the Marines after the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, and served four tours of duty in Iraq, was first elected to Massachusetts’ 6th Congressional District in 2014. He launched a 2020 presidential campaign but dropped it after a few months.
Markey was elected to the Senate in 2013. Before that he represented Massachusetts’ 7th Congressional District from 1976 to 2013.
Markey notably fended off a challenge in 2020 from Rep. Joe Kennedy III, a younger rival from one of the nation’s most famous political families. Markey did so by aligning himself with the liberal wing of the Democratic Party.
Antoine Hilaire, a 76-year-old Democrat who voted for Markey in Brockton on Tuesday, said being older can be a positive because it offers people experience and wisdom.
“If the older one is doing the better job, I don’t know,” he said. “He’s doing a good job. It’s not a big, big, big problem.”
Longtime Democratic House incumbents also face younger challengers
Lynch, 71, has held the 8th District seat in south Boston since 2001. He faced Roath, a 39-year-old lawyer who contended that it is time to end “wait-your-turn” politics. Lynch stressed the value of experience inside Congress.
Lynch has fended off other youth challenges in the past, but Roath’s campaign hoped for a boost of excitement after longtime Democratic incumbent U.S. Rep. John Larson was defeated by former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin in August in neighboring Connecticut. Like Roath, Bronin called for the need for generational change while running against an establishment politician.
Meanwhile the 1st District primary in western Massachusetts pitted Neal, 77, against Whalen, 39.
Neal, known as the dean of the New England House delegation, was first elected in 1988. Whalen ran to the left of Neal, calling for Medicare for All and questioning whether Neal has done enough to oppose Trump’s agenda.
Whalen recently was endorsed by Our Revolution, a progressive organization founded by Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont.

sources.news_title: Good Riddance, Seth Moulton: You Got What You Deserved
sources.text:
The biggest reason that Kamala Harris lost the 2024 election is probably the post-Covid-19 inflation and anti-incumbent sentiment that resulted in parties in power across the world being defeated. It didn’t help that she refused to distance herself from a deeply unpopular President Biden, ran on the “opportunity economy” and other banalities, and seemed more focused on courting the tiny fraction of Americans who are anti-Trump Republicans than any other bloc. But for many in the party, anytime the Democrats lose an election, the explanation is simple: Democrats are too far left. So in the days after Harris’s defeat, Democratic Representative Seth Moulton joined that chorus, telling The New York Times, “Democrats spend way too much time trying not to offend anyone rather than being brutally honest about the challenges many Americans face. I have two little girls. I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete, but as a Democrat I’m supposed to be afraid to say that.”
Transgender rights weren’t even close to the most prominent issue in the 2024 campaign. To the extent they were, it was a 2019 video of Harris supporting gender-affirming care for people in federal prison, a much harder position to defend than young people playing sports. It was strange that Moulton singled out transgender athletes for the Democrats’ defeat, as opposed to Biden, Harris, or their campaign strategists. Even worse, he whined when he was criticized for his remarks, suggesting those rebukes showed Democrats don’t tolerate alternative views. Moulton wanted to attack transgender participation in sports without those who support transgender athletes forcefully criticizing him in response. Sorry, Seth, that’s not how free speech or open discourse works.
Moulton exemplified the reactionary, left-bashing panic and capitulation to Trump we saw from many congressional Democrats in the wake of the 2024 election. Almost two years later, he got what he deserved: an electoral whupping. Incumbent Senator Ed Markey easily fended off Moulton’s primary challenge. The race was called quickly after polls closed on Tuesday night, and Markey is likely to win by more than 20 percentage points.
Moulton’s blowout loss, along with that of Angie Craig in Minnesota’s Senate race last month, should serve as a warning: Don’t expect to advance in Democratic politics, particularly in a blue state, if you spend the weeks after a Democratic presidential loss distancing yourself from the party base.
Defeating an incumbent senator is obviously hard, so Moulton’s loss isn’t shocking. But Moulton had a huge advantage in this race: age. Democratic voters, angered with Biden for initially running and then flopping on the debate state, are eager for generational change. So when Moulton, now 47, announced his challenge to Markey (80) back in October, I figured the congressman had the advantage.
In fact, it was an example of the scenario I feared. Early last year, some Democratic activists, furious about 2024, were arguing that any Democratic officeholder over age 70 should be replaced by someone younger. They’re wrong. What Democrats really need is not necessarily younger members but ones who fight hard, both for progressive policies and against Donald Trump and MAGA. I want Bernie Sanders (84) and Elizabeth Warren (77) on Capitol Hill, but not Josh Gottheimer (51) or Jared Golden (44). A fixation on age could elevate ambitious climbers who stand for nothing but their personal ambitions over the fighters we need to make America a better democracy.
But at least in Massachusetts, the younger candidate couldn’t hoodwink voters into thinking that he stands for change or fight or vigor. After all, this is Seth Moulton. He so perfectly embodies the hold-power, do-nothing ethos that plagues Democratic politics, which voters can easily discern. Despite serving in the House since 2015, he’s not been a prominent figure in fighting Trump. He didn’t propose anything particularly bold or creative during his brief 2020 presidential run. (You probably forgot that he ran.)
He likely only got on the radar of many Democrats in Massachusetts and nationally with his transgender comments. So when his campaign launched, progressive activists trashed him. “When people are talking about younger leadership stepping up, they’re talking about the Ayanna Pressleys, not the Seth Moultons,” Tanya Neslusan, executive director of MassEquality, a prominent LGBTQ+ rights group in Massachusetts, told NOTUS last fall.
And for an eightysomething, Markey was well positioned. Unlike Biden, he speaks clearly and walks confidently. He’s been a strong supporter of Medicare for All, the Green New Deal, and other left-wing policies, so progressives love him—including younger ones. Markey, not Moulton, was backed by Pressley, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, and numerous other younger Democratic politicians.
Markey took full advantage of Moulton’s transgender remarks, painting himself as the defender of the LGBTQ+ community and other groups that often face discrimination.
Moulton isn’t the only youngish Democrat who positioned himself rightward in the aftermath of the 2024 election and was rightly punished for it. Representative Angie Craig of Minnesota was one of 46 Democrats in the House and 12 in the Senate who voted for the Trump-backed Laken Riley Act, which calls for federal law enforcement to detain and deport immigrants charged with nonviolent crimes even before they are convicted. The legislation itself was bad. The message that those 58 Democrats wanted to send to the rest of the party was even worse: Trump had won the election, so Democrats needed to move right on immigration.
At best, those Democrats didn’t realize just how fervently anti-immigrant this administration would be. At worst, they further emboldened this administration by signaling that some Democrats wouldn’t object to heinous immigration law abuses.
Craig also ran for the Senate. And she lost the primary by 20 points, in part because Minnesota’s Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flaganan hammered Craig over her Laken Riley vote.
Most of the 58 Democrats who voted for the Laken Riley Act and otherwise capitulated to Trump early last year or blamed progressives for Harris’s defeat remain in Congress. But at least two are gone. And in Moulton’s case, this was an embarrassing defeat. Democrats in Massachusetts were so desperate not to have Seth Moulton be their senator that they were willing to overwhelmingly reelect an 80-year-old to a six-year term. Seth Moulton kicked trangender Americans and other progressives when they were down. Now, Massachusetts voters have kicked him out of politics. Job well done.

U.S. Sen. Ed Markey rolls to victory in Mass. Democratic primary
Voters stick with progressive stalwart and reject Moulton’s call for generational change
Sen. Ed Markey won the Democratic primary, fending off a challenger. (Photo by Michael Jonas)
This article first appeared on CommonWealth Beacon and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.
U.S. Sen. Ed Markey cruised to a decisive victory in Massachusetts’ Democratic primary against U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton, as voters soundly rejected the Salem congressman’s effort to turn the race into a referendum on Markey’s age.
In unofficial results on Tuesday night, Markey secured roughly 70% among Democratic primary voters to Moulton’s 30%.
It marked the second consecutive race in which Markey turned back a primary challenge from a younger member of the state’s congressional delegation. Six years ago, it was 39-year-old Joe Kennedy III who failed to make the case for generational change. This time, with Markey turning 80 during the heat of the primary campaign, it was the 47-year old Moulton who waged an ultimately losing bet that the senator had finally worn out his stay.
Moulton launched his campaign last October with a simple pitch — it was time to pass the torch.
Moulton, a Marine veteran who served four tours in Iraq, argued that it was time for a generational change in leadership and that he would bring fresh energy to the fight against President Trump and his agenda.
Markey pointed to his authorship of the Green New Deal, consistent progressive bona fides, and said he had never felt more energized about a campaign. He insisted repeatedly that it was not your age but the age of your ideas that was important, and then pointed to his long record of progressive policy battles.
Every public poll of the race showed Markey comfortably ahead.
After the candidates met for their first debate on July 8, the numbers barely wavered. A Suffolk University/Boston Globe poll found a majority of voters already leaning Markey by mid-August. A WBUR/UMass Amherst survey days later had him up nearly 30 points. The final Emerson College poll in late August put Markey at 60% to Moulton’s 33%. Women and voters under 40 — the exact voters Moulton needed to peel away — broke hardest for Markey, Emerson’s pollster said.
On policy, there was often little daylight between them — a point both men conceded across three debates.
Both called themselves the true progressive in the race and both back universal health care, though not the same version. Markey has embraced Medicare for All, a single-payer system, while Moulton favors a public option that would let a government plan compete alongside private insurers. Markey has also stayed tied to the Green New Deal, which he co-authored.
A major point of contention throughout the race was Moulton’s comments about transgender athletes shortly after President Trump’s 2024 victory, in which he talked about not wanting his daughters “getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete.” That prompted an apology from Moulton on the debate stage with Markey, and the incumbent senator accusing the congressman of “throwing trans kids under the bus.”
Markey’s sound win on Tuesday further signals that voters found him to be the unalloyed progressive, with Moulton’s comments around trans issues dogging him throughout the race.
Almost all of Markey’s fellow Massachusetts Democrats in Washington closed ranks, with six of the state’s eight House members and Sen. Elizabeth Warren endorsing him. Only Reps. Stephen Lynch and Jake Auchincloss stayed neutral, the Boston Globe reported.
Moulton’s most notable institutional counterweight came from The Boston Globe, which endorsed him over Markey. He also leaned on fellow veterans-turned-politicians who he helped elect nationally, including New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill.
Throughout the campaign, Markey cited his work with progressive star Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who was a prominent Markey backer against Kennedy in 2020. She held off on endorsing this time before backing him in the race’s final week.
Moulton had unseated an incumbent before, beating then-Rep. John Tierney in 2014. But his recent efforts to crack the party’s upper echelons and comments on trans young people in sports gave Markey’s allies ammunition to paint him as a striver out of step with Massachusetts priorities. In 2018, Moulton waged a failed attempt to block Nancy Pelosi from the speakership, and he made a short-lived 2020 presidential run.
Markey is a heavy favorite in November against Republican John Deaton, a Marine veteran and cryptocurrency attorney who lost to Sen. Elizabeth Warren by about 20 points in 2024. Massachusetts hasn’t sent a Republican to the Senate since Scott Brown’s 2010 special-election win. Brown’s DC tenure was brief. Two years later, Warren defeated him.

sources.news_title: Markey Defeats Moulton in Massachusetts Senate Primary
sources.text:
Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts has won Tuesday's Democratic Senate primary by a commanding margin, defeating Rep. Seth Moulton and handing the party's progressive wing one of its clearest victories of the 2026 midterm cycle. With early returns in, Markey was leading by nearly 50 percentage points — a result that exceeded even the most favorable pre-election polling and erased any residual uncertainty about which direction Massachusetts Democrats wanted to go.
The outcome was not, at its core, simply about Massachusetts. It was about what the Democratic Party primary electorate, energized and directional in ways not fully captured by generic ballot surveys, is willing to reward and what it will not.
The race was framed from its opening as a generational contest. Moulton, 47, announced his candidacy in October 2025 with an explicit argument that Markey, then 79, was too old to seek another six-year term. He invoked the experience of former President Biden's 2024 withdrawal, which Moulton had publicly supported, as evidence that age was a legitimate and urgent consideration for Democratic voters choosing their next standard-bearer. The pitch was calibrated and serious, and it reflected a genuine debate inside the party about longevity, relevance and the cost of incumbency in an era of rapid political change.
Massachusetts voters did not accept the premise. The final Emerson College poll before the primary found Markey leading 60 to 33 — a 30-point gap that had widened from a mere five-point Markey advantage in May. Among voters under 40, Markey led by 32 points. Among women, by 28. Moulton's strongest demographic was voters over 70, where he still trailed by 24 points. The generational argument, in other words, produced the opposite of the generational divide Moulton's campaign had anticipated. Younger Democratic primary voters rallied to the incumbent, not the challenger.
Part of the explanation lies in the endorsement architecture Markey assembled. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez all backed the incumbent, giving the campaign the institutional weight of the party's progressive infrastructure at a moment when that infrastructure was highly motivated. Markey, who has served in Congress since the Carter administration and co-authored the Green New Deal resolution with Ocasio-Cortez, remained a totemic figure for a Democratic base that prioritized ideological alignment over generational turnover.
The deeper explanation, however, runs through the Strait of Hormuz. The Iran war, now six months old and broadly unpopular among Democratic voters, became the sharpest dividing line between the two candidates. Markey ran explicitly against the conflict, positioning himself as a consistent antiwar voice in a Senate where the administration's war powers have faced limited institutional challenge. Moulton, a Marine Corps combat veteran and member of the House Armed Services Committee, took a more calibrated approach — critical of aspects of the administration's handling of the war but unwilling to call for its end and deeply skeptical of rapid disengagement from a volatile regional situation.
Whether Massachusetts Democratic primary voters read that difference as a principled national security posture or as insufficient opposition to an unpopular war is a question the margin suggests they resolved decisively. Markey's near-50-point win arrived on the same day that U.S. Central Command announced a fresh wave of strikes against Iranian targets, oil prices pushed above $90 a barrel, and a Reuters/Ipsos poll placed Trump's approval at 33 percent — the lowest of his second term. The political environment in which Tuesday's primary was decided was not a neutral backdrop. It was an active argument in favor of the candidate who had staked out the clearer antiwar position.
The Massachusetts result does not exist in isolation. Other longtime Democratic incumbents have lost to younger challengers in primaries earlier this cycle, and Moulton's campaign had pointed to those results as evidence that the political winds had shifted against incumbency. The Massachusetts outcome complicates that narrative without fully resolving it. What it does suggest is that the antiwar, progressive lane remains viable and potent in Democratic primaries, and that the national security centrist argument — however coherent on its own terms — faces structural headwinds in a party whose primary electorate is currently animated by opposition to a war it largely does not support.
For Moulton, Tuesday's result is a significant setback. He had positioned this race as a generational argument that the party needed to have, and the party declined the invitation by an unusually wide margin. His political future — whether in his current House seat, in another statewide race, or in a repositioned role within the national conversation — will be shaped by how he processes a loss this definitive.
For Markey, the path now leads to November and a general election in a state that has not elected a Republican senator since 1972. The competitive question was always Tuesday. He answered it with room to spare. What the margin means for the broader Democratic coalition, for the party's positioning on the Iran war heading into the final stretch before November, and for the progressive infrastructure that delivered it — those are the questions that will take longer to answer, and that other campaigns in other states are already trying to work out.

sources.news_title: Markey overcomes Senate challenge - The Daily Bo Snerdley
sources.text:
(The Center Square) – Octogenerian U.S. Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., overcame an intense primary challenge from a candidate who said he was too old to serve the people of Massachusetts.
Markey, 80, secured election for a third full term on Tuesday night, overcoming a challenge from insurgent candidate Seth Moulton. The incumbent senator focused his campaign on fiercely advocating for progressive values, pointing to his support of the Green New Deal, Medicare for All legislation and calls to abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
“We don’t just need a Democratic majority in the Senate,” Markey said. “We need a progressive majority. That’s why I’m working to take on this corrupt administration and build a better future for working class Americans.”
Markey pledged this term would be his final one in office if elected. Moulton, 47, had fiercely attacked Markey’s age and called for new leadership in Congress.
Moulton said Markey is not prepared to advance regulations on new technology advances, including in artificial intelligence. He called for federal AI regulations, including bans on data harvesting, protections for children and unemployment insurance, while keeping the technology based in the United States.
“We can’t let China dominate this technology, but we also cannot allow AI systems to be deployed unless they are safe,” Moulton’s website reads. “The best version of American leadership means winning and doing it right.”
Markey hit back at Moulton and touted his record to advance regulations on bias in AI generation. His legislation called for ensuring algorithms used in AI tools do not reflect or exacerbate preexisting biases when used in the hiring process, for example.
“A 2025 study found that AI resume screening tools almost never selected Black male names to proceed in the hiring process,” Markey said in a press conference. “This is unacceptable.”
Markey will face off against Republican candidate John Deaton, a trial attorney who has focused his campaign on increasing healthcare affordability. He has slammed Democrats who proposed Medicare for All legislation and called for proposals that do not substantially raise taxes for Massachusetts residents.
“I’ll work to lower prescription drug costs, increase price transparency, and expand access to quality care without growing Washington’s bureaucracy or raising taxes,” Deaton’s website reads.
U.S. House
Several races across Massachusetts for the U.S. House saw tense challenges against incumbent Democrats as well. Here is a look at some of those races.
District 1
Incumbent Democrat Rep. Richard Neal, was leading against a challenge from progressive Jeromie Whalen with 7% of precincts reporting. Neal, 77, is seeking his 18th consecutive term in the U.S. House.
The incumbent Democrat focused his campaign on fighting against the Trump administration’s tax and tariff policies. He touted his record as chairman of the Joint Committee on Taxation in the 117th Congress.
“Congressman Neal has been an advocate of fairness and simplification of the U.S. tax code, supporter of policies that increase the national savings rate, and fought relentlessly to protect Social Security and Medicare from privatization,” Neal’s website reads.
Whalen, a 39-year-old high school teacher, has focused his campaign on Medicare for All and the Fair Share Amendment, a Massachusetts amendment that funds public education and transportation through taxation on high-income earners.
“Raise the tax threshold for working and middle class: Create a Cost of Living Exemption so that federal taxes do not apply to income up to a realistic cost of living for a single adult, set around $45,000 per year,” Whalen told Ballotpedia. “Surcharge on the ultra wealthy: Add a 3 percent surtax on income over $1 million, and an 8 percent surtax on income over $15 million.”
A Republican candidate in the first congressional district did not file for election. The winning Democrat will is expected to win the seat unless a mass write-in campaign overtakes him.
District 6
No clear winner emerged atop a crowded field of Democratic primary contenders early Tuesday night in a race to face off against Republican Micah Jones in November.
Dan Koh, who was endorsed by President Joe Biden, was in a favored lead with 13% of precincts reporting over state Rep. Tram Nguyen, software engineer Beth Andres-Beck and attorney John Beccia. Koh focused his campaign on fighting back against the Trump administration, expanding healthcare and childcare and supporting affordable housing.
“Everyone who works hard should have a fair shot at building a good life,” Koh told Ballotpedia. “I’ve seen firsthand how government can make people’s lives better when it focuses on real challenges and real solutions.”
Nguyen, a member of the Massachusetts legislature, has championed progressive values throughout her campaign. She focused on Medicare for All, increasing the federal minimum wage and expanding affordable housing opportunities.
“In Congress, Tram will work to: Significantly expand funding for deeply affordable housing and rental assistance, Increase the affordable housing supply, Support first-time home buyers with low interest loans and developing more starter homes,” Nguyen told Ballotpedia.
The winning Democrat will face off against Republican Micah Jones, a lawyer, who has focused his campaign on reducing tax burdens and focusing on AI legislation.
“Eliminating unnecessary barriers to economic growth, encouraging common sense innovation in areas like artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing, expanding clean and reliable energy, and creating more pathways for young Americans to serve their communities and develop valuable career skills,” Jones told Ballotpedia.
District 8
The race for Massachusetts’ eighth congressional district was still awaiting results early Tuesday night Incumbent Rep. Stephen Lynch, D-Mass., and Patrick Roath, a lawyer and aide to former Massachusetts Gov. Deval Patrick are in the race for the Democratic ticket
Lynch focused his campaign on touting his voting record and his pursuit of President Donald Trump. However, Roath sharply criticized Lynch for not doing enough to aggressively go after the president.
“I’ve worked every day in Congress for policies that will make life better for you and your family – fair wages and economic security, funding for higher education, housing assistance, preserving Social Security, protecting against threats to our environment, and health care that is affordable and accessible,” Lynch’s website reads.
Roath also supported expansion of the Fair Share Amendment beyond Massachusetts and across the country.
“Every American worker deserves what we’ve already achieved here–12 weeks of guaranteed paid family leave, regardless of whether you work for a corporation or a small business, whether you’re salaried or hourly,” Roath wrote.
The winning Democratic candidate will face off against Republican Robert Burke, who ran unopposed and called for a complete immigration pause across the country.
“It’s time to reevaluate every program, from H1B to TPS, prioritizing American interests, border security, and a balanced system that truly serves our nation’s needs,” Burke’s website reads.

sources.text:
Markey coasts to victory over Moulton in Massachusetts primary
It’s a good night for Democratic incumbents as Reps. Lynch and Neal also prevail
Sen. Edward J. Markey, the 80-year-old progressive stalwart from Massachusetts, sailed to victory in his Democratic primary Tuesday as a pair of septuagenarian House Democrats turned back younger challengers.
With their victories, Reps. Stephen F. Lynch and Richard E. Neal avoided joining the seven House Democrats to lose primary challenges this year, mostly to progressive and younger rivals.
In the Senate race, Markey was leading Rep. Seth Moulton, whose campaign was built on a call for generational change, 65 percent to 35 percent, with 81 percent of the vote in, according to The Associated Press.
“Tonight is a testament to the power of the progressive movement of our nation,’’ Markey told supporters in Boston. “It is a progressive movement fueled by young people demanding more from their leaders, and it’s your voices that are the ones we need to hear right now. Your leadership will show us the way.”
In deep-blue Massachusetts, Markey will be heavily favored to win in November against Marine Corps veteran John Deaton, who was unopposed for the Republican nomination. Deaton was also the losing GOP nominee to Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren in 2024.
If he wins, Markey has pledged to serve one last term, at the end of which he would be 86.
A push for generational change has surged through Democratic politics this year, as the party continues to grapple with the fallout from Joe Biden’s ill-fated 2024 reelection campaign. Among the House Democrats who lost their bids for renomination this year, most were felled by opponents running to their left.
But in Massachusetts, it was Markey who assumed the progressive mantle against 47-year-old Moulton, highlighting his legislative record and his calls to abolish the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency and pass “Medicare for All.”
He also embraced transgender rights, criticizing Moulton for saying after the 2024 election that he didn’t want his daughters “getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete.” (Moulton later apologized.)
Markey relied on support from progressive allies, such as Reps. Ayanna S. Pressley and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders, as well as an army of young volunteers.
Moulton made Markey’s age the focus of his campaign, asserting that it was “time for a new generation of leadership to take on a new generation of challenges and opportunities.” At a recent debate, Markey was asked whether he used artificial intelligence. “I use whatever is inside my iPhone or my iPad, whatever comes up,” he responded.
To Moulton, Markey’s halting answer signified the senator’s failure to grasp an essential technology reshaping American society, and it was quickly repurposed for a digital ad.
Moulton’s career has been marked by a willingness to do battle with his party’s elders. In 2014, he won his North Shore congressional seat after dislodging a nine-term Democratic incumbent. A few years later, he led an ultimately unsuccessful uprising against incoming Speaker Nancy Pelosi, then the party’s most powerful woman. And a year after that, he took a stab at running for president; his long-shot bid lasted all of four months.
“Challenging the establishment and calling for a new generation of leadership isn’t easy, but it is necessary. We started conversations that needed to happen, and I will never stop pushing the Democratic Party and our country to look toward the future,’’ Moulton told supporters in Dorchester. “We didn’t achieve our goal tonight, but I am confident that because of this campaign, others will be inspired to buck the system when they’re told to wait their turn.”
Markey was first elected to the Massachusetts legislature when Richard M. Nixon served in the White House, then came to the House in 1976 and moved to the Senate after winning a special election in 2013.
This isn’t the first time he has faced a younger Democrat seeking to harness dissatisfaction with the gerontocracy in Washington. In 2020, he was challenged by -Rep. Joseph P. Kennedy III. The result was less lopsided: Markey won by about 10 points, handing the Kennedy family its first loss in a Massachusetts election.
House races
In the 8th District, Lynch, 71, staved off challenger Patrick Roath, a 39-year-old lawyer and voting rights activist from Jamaica Plain.
With just under 80 percent of votes counted, Lynch was leading Roath 57 percent to 43 percent, the AP reported early Wednesday morning.
Roath, who had the backing of Leaders We Deserve, a political group founded by Gen Z activist David Hogg, outraised the incumbent during the campaign and criticized his at-times moderate voting record as out of step with the politics of the district.
But Lynch, a former ironworker from South Boston who was first elected to the House in 2001, focused on his seniority and his working-class background.
In the 1st District in Western Massachusetts, Neal, 77, defeated 39-year-old teacher Jeromie Whalen. But the margin was closer than expected, considering the incumbent’s towering fundraising advantage over his challenger. With an estimated 90 percent of votes in, Neal was leading Whalen 54 percent to 46 percent, the AP reported early Wednesday morning.
Still, the result appears to be the closest primary race of Neal’s near-four-decade congressional career. As the top Democrat on the powerful Ways and Means Committee, Neal emphasized the millions of dollars he’s brought back to the district as he campaigned for a 20th term. He also significantly outraised Whalen, who ran a grassroots campaign from his canary-yellow Toyota cargo van.
Other House Democrats who easily turned back primary challenges Tuesday included House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, Rep. William Keating and Rep. Jake Auchincloss.
And in the race to succeed Moulton, former Biden White House adviser Dan Koh beat out a crowd of Democrats vying for 6th District in the state’s North Shore.
Koh, who also worked for former Labor Secretary and former Boston Mayor Martin J. Walsh, was leading the field with 41 percent, just after midnight Wednesday, according to the AP. His nearest challenger, state Rep. Tram Nguyen, lagged more than 10 points behind.
The contest marked Koh’s second run for Congress. He sought the nearby 3rd District seat in 2018, narrowly losing the Democratic nomination to Lori Trahan. In this race, Trahan endorsed Nguyen, while Koh touted endorsements from former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris. He also had the support of former Rep. John F. Tierney, who held the seat before Moulton.
Koh is favored to prevail over Republican Army veteran Micah Jones in the general election for the deep-blue seat. Victory would make Koh, who is of Korean and Lebanese descent, the first Asian American to represent Massachusetts in Congress.

Markey Defeats Moulton in Democratic Primary
Incumbent Senator Ed J. Markey (D-Mass.) secured the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate on Tuesday, beating Representative Seth W. Moulton ’01 (D-Mass.) after a campaign centered on generational turnover.
The 80-year-old candidate secured 76 percent of the vote, according to the Associated Press, and will now face Republican candidate John Deaton in the November general election in pursuit of his third Senate term.
Moulton represents the Sixth Congressional District of Massachusetts, which stretches from Salem to Amesbury. Moulton launched his campaign against Markey last October, arguing that Markey was too old to run for re-election.
Though Moulton is viewed as a more moderate Democrat, he and Markey are generally aligned on policy issues, leaving age as the most prominent distinction between the two. In his campaign announcement, 47-year-old Moulton compared Markey’s candidacy to former U.S. President Joe Biden’s unsuccessful 2024 presidential campaign, which sparked turmoil in the Democratic party over lawmakers’ ages and generational differences.
Markey has served in Congress for nearly 50 years and was first elected to the Senate in 2013. If elected in November, he will be 86 by the end of his next term.
Moulton’s campaign was not the first time Markey, the oldest Senate Democrat seeking reelection in the midterms, faced a challenge largely centered on his age. Joseph P. Kennedy III challenged Markey for Senate in 2020, similarly calling for younger leadership. Kennedy lost the primary by 11 points.
Moulton came under scrutiny in early August when The American Prospect published an investigation, cited by the Markey campaign, alleging Moulton made millions while serving on the House Armed Services Committee through private business dealings.
Moulton has faced criticism from more progressive Democrats for his 2024 comments opposing the participation of transgender athletes in women’s sports. He apologized for his comments at a recent debate, but Markey’s campaign invoked the comments repeatedly throughout the campaign.

Moulton also clashed with the party last fall after Democrats approved the 2026 federal budget, a Senate bill that would reopen the government after a 43-day shutdown. Moulton slammed his fellow Democrats in a November interview with The Crimson for approving the bill without renewing the expiring subsidies for health insurance premiums on the Affordable Care Act market.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) He was also supported by Boston Mayor Michelle Wu ’07, Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea J. Campbell, and all but one Boston city councilor.

An Aug. 26 poll conducted by 7NEWS and the University of New Hampshire showed Markey with a 35-point lead.
Moulton still outraised Markey by nearly $1 million. He raised more than $6.2 million for his campaign, including more than $241,000 from PACs. Markey raised nearly $5.4 million and received nearly $590,000 from PACs.
Markey has represented Massachusetts in the Senate since a June 2013 special election after former Senator John Kerry resigned to become Secretary of State. He has built his Senate career largely around climate policy, co-authoring the Green New Deal resolution with Rep. Ocasio-Cortez in 2019.

sources.news_title: Markey wins Massachusetts Democratic primary, calls to stop Gaza bombing
sources.text:
Massachusetts progressive Sen. Ed Markey, a sharp critic of Israel, beat the more moderate Rep. Seth Moulton by a wide margin on Tuesday, securing the Democratic nomination for the upcoming U.S. Senate race.
The Associated Press called the race just a half hour after polls closed, at 8:31 p.m. By Wednesday morning, with 96% of the vote counted, according to AP, Markey had secured 64.9% of votes to Moulton’s 35.1%.
“Tonight is a testament to the power of the progressive movement,” Markey said in his victory speech Tuesday. “It is a progressive movement fueled by young people demanding more from their leaders.”
Markey focused primarily on domestic issues in his remarks but briefly mentioned the Middle East. “We need to end the war in Iran, and stop the bombing in Gaza,” Markey said. “We need to slash the Pentagon budget.”
Noting that he spoke to Moulton prior to taking the stage, Markey added that he looks forward to working together “to build a better future for everyone.”
Moulton, meanwhile, told his supporters that he had “called Sen. Markey to congratulate him on his victory tonight.” He conveyed his “full support” for his opponent as the Democratic nominee, stressing that they “must stand united this November to protect our democracy and defeat Donald Trump.”
Markey, 80, began serving in the U.S. House of Representatives 50 years ago and remained there until he was elected to fill the Senate seat of John Kerry, who was appointed U.S. Secretary of State in 2013. During Markey’s time in the House, he was a member of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, and in the Senate, he has supported multiple resolutions aimed at cutting military aid and munitions sales to Israel.
Moulton, 47, was born two years after Markey arrived on Capitol Hill. He has been serving in the U.S. House since 2015 and has opposed both the Democratic socialist agenda and the aging establishment, instead calling for “new energy, new ideas and leaders willing to put people over politics.”
“We ran a race that stood on principle, that wasn’t just about politics as usual, and that elevated the voices of Massachusetts citizens who have been left behind by the status quo in Washington,” Moulton said on Tuesday. “Challenging the establishment and calling for a new generation of leadership isn’t easy, but it is necessary,” he added.
Many political analysts have suggested that Moulton’s predominant focus on his youth and his opponent’s age may have been his primary downfall. Although in the weeks leading up the primary, polls had projected Markey’s win, the two candidates had been running neck-and-neck in the preceding months.
A New York Times opinion piece recently described Moulton as a “rebel without a cause” who drifted with “the political winds” and focused on platforms he was fighting against rather than those he was supporting. 
Moulton was an early moderate Democrat to reject AIPAC  funding. He declared in October that he was “returning AIPAC donations” and refusing new funds from the pro-Israel lobby. 
“In recent years AIPAC has aligned itself too closely with Prime Minister Netanyahu’s government,” Moulton posted at the time. “I’m a friend of Israel, but not of its current government.”
Track AIPAC, a group that documents political spending by pro-Israel lobbies, reported that such PACs have spent about $101,500 on Moulton over his career — a relatively modest amount for a six-term congressman.
“It is clearly the safe thing to do, if you are running for a nomination in the Democratic Party, to aggressively distance yourself from Israel,” Jeff Robbins, a Boston-based attorney and former Senate investigative counsel, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency.
Robbins, who also served as delegate to the United Nations Human Rights Commission under President Bill Clinton, described the shift as “reflective of the reality that we have seen play out in spades over the last year.”
That situation involves Democratic candidates “running for the hills about AIPAC and treating it as a boogeyman,” added Robbins, who began organizing pro-Israel rallies in in 2012, while chairing the New England Board of the Anti-Defamation League.
“If you want to have a prayer of being elected in a Democratic primary in this country, you had better be able to say, ‘I don’t take money from AIPAC. In fact, I never heard of it before,’” he added.

sources.text:
Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) easily fended off a primary challenge from Rep. Seth Moulton (D-Mass.), who made the 80-year-old progressive senator’s age a top issue.
The Associated Press called the race for Markey at 8:31 pm. With just three percent of the vote counted, Markey led with 74.2 percent to Moulton’s 25.8 percent.
The race was an outlier from the norms seen in Democratic races this cycle.
But in the Massachusetts Senate race this year, that was turned on its head.
In this contest, the octogenarian Markey—who has made a career boosting environmentalist initiatives such as the Green New Deal and anti-Big Oil stances—was widely seen as the more progressive pick. He won key progressive endorsements from figures including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), who sponsored the Green New Deal in the House, and Senate heavyweights such as Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.).
Meanwhile, Moulton is widely seen as the more centrist figure.
Markey agreed with a reporter’s question about whether Moulton is “too moderate” for Massachusetts, noting that the challenger had opposed Medicare for All in the past.
Moulton has pressed the age argument in the campaign’s final stretch.
“The world has changed, and Senator Markey is very much running the same campaign he did back in 2020,” Moulton told CBS’s “Face the Nation” on Aug. 23.
He pointed to a moment in a recent debate in which he said Markey, asked whether he used artificial intelligence, responded that he used “whatever is inside of [his] iPhone and [his] iPad, whatever comes up.”
“The world has just moved on,” Moulton said. “It’s not a personal thing with Ed Markey. It’s about whether one Senate seat should belong to one person while the world is moving on without him.”
Markey has shot back against these criticisms, telling reporters at the U.S. Capitol, “It’s not your age, it’s the age of your ideas.”
He said that in this respect, “I’m the youngest guy in the race.”
Though the race had drawn national attention for its unusual age and political dynamics, the result ultimately came as little surprise: Markey had been overwhelmingly favored to win the contest, having led by double-digit margins in every poll conducted of the race.
He also maintained strong support from the state-level Democratic Party. A majority of delegates to the state party convention in May voted to endorse him, though Moulton drew enough support to qualify for the ballot.
“Massachusetts is testing whether generational change is actually an ideology or merely an attribute,” said Michael Fahey, founder and CEO of Fahey Communications. He’s a Boston political and public relations strategist and former television news executive who covered both men as a journalist.
“In many Democratic primaries, younger challengers have succeeded because youth came packaged with a different ideological vision. Massachusetts is different. Moulton has the generational argument, while Markey has the stronger claim on the progressive movement.”
Markey, who first entered the Senate in 2013 after nearly 37 years in the House, has faced similar electoral challenges based on his age before this one.
In 2020, he turned back a primary challenge from then-Rep. Joseph Kennedy III, 55 percent to 45 percent, running with the backing of younger progressives and campaigning on the Green New Deal.
However, the issue drew greater attention this time in part due to the lingering impacts of the 2024 election, when questions about former President Joe Biden’s age ultimately forced him to depart the race months before the election.
“Moulton’s age argument is still more potent today than it would have been six years ago. Joe Biden fundamentally changed how voters think about age, capacity and longevity in public office,” Fahey said. “But politically, Moulton has to turn age into consequence.”

Markey co-sponsored the Green New Deal, supported Medicare for All and received endorsements from independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, Democratic New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Democratic Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren and “Squad” member Democratic Massachusetts Rep. Ayanna Pressley. Further-left candidates have won several races and defeated incumbents throughout the 2026 cycle, including Democratic Colorado congressional candidate Melat Kiros, who defeated longtime incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette in July. (RELATED: Democrat Voters Replacing Old Guard Far Faster Than GOP)
.@EdMarkey (D-MA) calls for Trump to be impeached and for ICE to be abolished: "We need to slash the defense budget and we need to impeach Donald Trump now." pic.twitter.com/qLZ3QB3DaN
— CSPAN (@cspan) August 29, 2026
The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) is on pace to field its largest congressional delegation in its history. Young, college-educated voters have turned out in droves to support younger, more progressive candidates.
It is less common for older incumbents to defeat their younger opponents in recent Democratic primaries. Democratic Reps. Shri Thanedar of Michigan, John Larson of Connecticut and Adriano Espaillat of New York — who are all over the age of 70 — all lost their races to younger candidates.
“Democratic voters are hungry for a new generation of leaders who can credibly argue they’ll fight for change” Amanda Litman, founder of left-wing group Run For Something, told Axios.
Moulton ran as the moderate, receiving endorsements from Democratic New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, Democratic New York Rep. Pat Ryan and Democratic Rhode Island Rep. Seth Magaziner, according to his campaign website. He campaigned on affordability, outlined a plan for encounters with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and creating a public option for healthcare.
Markey supports allowing irreversible procedures for trans-identifying minors, abolishing ICE and implementing “universal healthcare,” according to his campaign website.
This is the second consecutive election cycle in which Markey prevailed against a younger challenger. In 2020, the then-74-year-old senator defeated then-39-year-old Rep. Joe Kennedy III — the nephew of now Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. —in the Democratic Senate primary.
Markey has held elected political office since 1973, when Richard Nixon was president — five years before Moulton was born. He served in the Massachusetts State House from that year to 1976, the U.S. House from 1976 to 2013 and the Senate since 2013.
Some older House Democrats faced pressure to drop out and ultimately did not run for reelection. These Democrats included Jerry Nadler of New York, Steve Cohen of Tennessee, Lloyd Doggett of Texas and Eleanor Holmes Norton. Cohen faced a primary challenge from 31-year-old Tennessee state Rep. Justin Pearson, and ultimately dropped out after Tennessee redrew his district’s lines.
