sources.text:
(The Center Square) - Octogenerian U.S. Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., overcame an intense primary challenge from a candidate who said he was too old to serve the people of Massachusetts.
Markey, 80, secured election for a third full term on Tuesday night, overcoming a challenge from insurgent candidate Seth Moulton. The incumbent senator focused his campaign on fiercely advocating for progressive values, pointing to his support of the Green New Deal, Medicare for All legislation and calls to abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
“We don’t just need a Democratic majority in the Senate,” Markey said. “We need a progressive majority. That’s why I’m working to take on this corrupt administration and build a better future for working class Americans.”
Markey pledged this term would be his final one in office if elected. Moulton, 47, had fiercely attacked Markey’s age and called for new leadership in Congress.
Moulton said Markey is not prepared to advance regulations on new technology advances, including in artificial intelligence. He called for federal AI regulations, including bans on data harvesting, protections for children and unemployment insurance, while keeping the technology based in the United States.
“We can’t let China dominate this technology, but we also cannot allow AI systems to be deployed unless they are safe,” Moulton’s website reads. “The best version of American leadership means winning and doing it right.”
Markey hit back at Moulton and touted his record to advance regulations on bias in AI generation. His legislation called for ensuring algorithms used in AI tools do not reflect or exacerbate preexisting biases when used in the hiring process, for example.
“A 2025 study found that AI resume screening tools almost never selected Black male names to proceed in the hiring process,” Markey said in a press conference. “This is unacceptable.”
Markey will face off against Republican candidate John Deaton, a trial attorney who has focused his campaign on increasing healthcare affordability. He has slammed Democrats who proposed Medicare for All legislation and called for proposals that do not substantially raise taxes for Massachusetts residents.
“I’ll work to lower prescription drug costs, increase price transparency, and expand access to quality care without growing Washington’s bureaucracy or raising taxes,” Deaton’s website reads.
U.S. House
Several races across Massachusetts for the U.S. House saw tense challenges against incumbent Democrats as well. Here is a look at some of those races.
District 1
Incumbent Democrat Rep. Richard Neal, was leading against a challenge from progressive Jeromie Whalen with 7% of precincts reporting. Neal, 77, is seeking his 18th consecutive term in the U.S. House.
The incumbent Democrat focused his campaign on fighting against the Trump administration’s tax and tariff policies. He touted his record as chairman of the Joint Committee on Taxation in the 117th Congress.
“Congressman Neal has been an advocate of fairness and simplification of the U.S. tax code, supporter of policies that increase the national savings rate, and fought relentlessly to protect Social Security and Medicare from privatization,” Neal’s website reads.
Whalen, a 39-year-old high school teacher, has focused his campaign on Medicare for All and the Fair Share Amendment, a Massachusetts amendment that funds public education and transportation through taxation on high-income earners.
“Raise the tax threshold for working and middle class: Create a Cost of Living Exemption so that federal taxes do not apply to income up to a realistic cost of living for a single adult, set around $45,000 per year,” Whalen told Ballotpedia. “Surcharge on the ultra wealthy: Add a 3 percent surtax on income over $1 million, and an 8 percent surtax on income over $15 million.”
A Republican candidate in the first congressional district did not file for election. The winning Democrat will is expected to win the seat unless a mass write-in campaign overtakes him.
District 6
No clear winner emerged atop a crowded field of Democratic primary contenders early Tuesday night in a race to face off against Republican Micah Jones in November.
Dan Koh, who was endorsed by President Joe Biden, was in a favored lead with 13% of precincts reporting over state Rep. Tram Nguyen, software engineer Beth Andres-Beck and attorney John Beccia. Koh focused his campaign on fighting back against the Trump administration, expanding healthcare and childcare and supporting affordable housing.
“Everyone who works hard should have a fair shot at building a good life,” Koh told Ballotpedia. “I’ve seen firsthand how government can make people’s lives better when it focuses on real challenges and real solutions.”
Nguyen, a member of the Massachusetts legislature, has championed progressive values throughout her campaign. She focused on Medicare for All, increasing the federal minimum wage and expanding affordable housing opportunities.
“In Congress, Tram will work to: Significantly expand funding for deeply affordable housing and rental assistance, Increase the affordable housing supply, Support first-time home buyers with low interest loans and developing more starter homes,” Nguyen told Ballotpedia.
The winning Democrat will face off against Republican Micah Jones, a lawyer, who has focused his campaign on reducing tax burdens and focusing on AI legislation.
“Eliminating unnecessary barriers to economic growth, encouraging common sense innovation in areas like artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing, expanding clean and reliable energy, and creating more pathways for young Americans to serve their communities and develop valuable career skills,” Jones told Ballotpedia.
District 8
The race for Massachusetts' eighth congressional district was still awaiting results early Tuesday night Incumbent Rep. Stephen Lynch, D-Mass., and Patrick Roath, a lawyer and aide to former Massachusetts Gov. Deval Patrick are in the race for the Democratic ticket
Lynch focused his campaign on touting his voting record and his pursuit of President Donald Trump. However, Roath sharply criticized Lynch for not doing enough to aggressively go after the president.
“I’ve worked every day in Congress for policies that will make life better for you and your family – fair wages and economic security, funding for higher education, housing assistance, preserving Social Security, protecting against threats to our environment, and health care that is affordable and accessible,” Lynch’s website reads.
Roath also supported expansion of the Fair Share Amendment beyond Massachusetts and across the country.
“Every American worker deserves what we've already achieved here–12 weeks of guaranteed paid family leave, regardless of whether you work for a corporation or a small business, whether you’re salaried or hourly,” Roath wrote.
The winning Democratic candidate will face off against Republican Robert Burke, who ran unopposed and called for a complete immigration pause across the country.
“It’s time to reevaluate every program, from H1B to TPS, prioritizing American interests, border security, and a balanced system that truly serves our nation’s needs,” Burke’s website reads.

sources.news_title: ‘A testament to the power of the progressive movement’: Markey beats Moulton in US Senate primary
sources.text:
Massachusetts Sen. Ed Markey defeated Rep. Seth Moulton in a sharply contested Democratic primary Tuesday.
The incumbent senator will face Republican John Deaton in November.
While Moulton made generational change the focus of his campaign — he is 47, and Markey is 80 — Markey won by casting himself as a champion of the party’s younger, left-leaning activists.
“Tonight is a testament to the power of the progressive movement of our nation,” Markey said in his victory speech in downtown Boston. “It is a progressive movement fueled by young people demanding more from their leaders, and it’s your voices that are the ones we need to hear right now.”
Markey promised on the campaign trail in 2026 that this six-year term would be his last.
It was the second consecutive Senate election cycle in which Markey fended off a significantly younger challenger. He defeated then-Rep. Joe Kennedy III in 2020.
As of 5:45 a.m., with 96% of the votes counted, Markey was leading with 65% of the vote compared to 35% for Moulton.
Tali Zechory, a Markey supporter from Cambridge, cited his support for the transgender community.
“I think he’s a great champion of progressive causes,” Zechory said of Markey. “I think he’s not afraid to stand up for those more vulnerable and targeted, especially when those communities can become so easily scapegoated.”
Zechory said she was referring to Moulton’s controversial comments in an interview with the New York Times in 2024, in an article when Democratic leaders and insiders were deconstructing why Kamala Harris fell to President Donald Trump.
“I have two little girls. I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete. But as a Democrat, I’m supposed to be afraid to say that,” Moulton told the Times in 2024.
Laurie and Raymond Ball, a Newton couple, were also in attendance at Markey’s primary-night gathering in downtown Boston. Like Zechory, they’d never been to a politics watch party before.
Laurie Ball, who was wearing an LGBTQ+ Star of David, said she’s supporting Markey because their child is a trans young adult. She said she’s grateful to Markey for his impassioned support of the transgender community.
“Moulton made a mistake,” she said.
While Moulton has consistently voted in support of LGBTQ+ issues and offered a qualified apology to the transgender community for his remarks in a debate this summer, he struggled to regain trust with LGBTQ+ supporters ever since his remarks to the Times.
Raymond Ball, a retired environmental engineer, also liked that Markey was a strong supporter of the Green New Deal.
The significance that trans rights played in the primary contest was underscored by the first speaker to introduce Markey — Tyler Hack, the executive director of the Christopher Street Project, which works to build trans political power.
Hack called Markey a steadfast ally at a time when other politicians seem to see trans rights as negotiable.
“To every trans kid who’s watching today, Massachusetts has a message for you,” Hack said. “You are going to grow up, and there are people will fight like hell to make sure you are able to. One of them is Senator Ed Markey.”
At Moulton’s party in Dorchester, the North Shore congressman took the stage to address his supporters.
“I just called Senator Markey to congratulate him on his victory tonight,” Moulton told the crowd. “He has my full support as our Democratic nominee, and we must stand united this November to protect our democracy and defeat Donald Trump.
“We entered this race as the underdog, and while tonight’s outcome isn’t what we worked so hard to achieve, I could not be prouder of the campaign we built together,” Moulton said. “Challenging the establishment and calling for a new generation of leadership isn’t easy, but it is necessary. We started conversations that needed to happen, and I will never stop pushing the Democratic Party and our country to look toward the future.”
Moulton’s backers are disappointed.
“I hope he runs again. He has so much to give,” Nancy Perkins, a retired music therapist from Andover, told GBH News.
All over the union hall, supporters are saying the same thing: “Seth just has to run again.”

sources.text:
Incumbent Ed Markey, 80, defeats Seth Moulton, 47, in Massachusetts Democratic Senate primary
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Add The New York Post on Google
Incumbent Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) easily defeated a much younger challenger Tuesday in Massachusetts’ Democratic Senate primary.
Markey, 80, topped Rep. Seth Moulton (D-Mass.) in a 76%-24% vote. He will face Republican John Deaton in November.
The race centered on whether Markey was too old to serve a third term in the Senate. If he wins re-election, the longtime liberal stalwart will be 86 by the end of his next term.
“Is he too old? Look, every political consultant will tell me not to say this, but the honest truth is, yes,” Moulton, 47, told the Boston Globe last fall, when asked about Markey during his campaign launch.
Moulton, a six-term congressman and one of the first House Democrats to call for former President Joe Biden to end his re-election bid over concerns about his age and mental acuity, seized on Markey stumbling over a recent debate question about artificial intelligence to highlight the need for a generational change.
When asked last week if he uses Claude or ChatGPT, Markey seemed completely oblivious to the AI platforms.
“I use whatever is inside of my iPhone or my iPad — whatever comes up, and I don’t know what companies my iPad may be using,” the senator responded.
Moulton shot back: “With all due respect, senator, if you don’t even know what you’re using on your phone or your iPad, like, this is why we need a new generation of leaders.”
The congressman further argued that “not understanding the basics of AI – the most important technology of our lifetime – should be disqualifying for a US Senator.”
Markey, however, had strong support from both far-left and establishment elements of the Democratic Party.
The incumbent’s campaign received a $62,000 boost from the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), the campaign arm of Senate Democrats, less than three weeks before Election Day.
Markey received endorsements from socialist Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), “Squad” Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
The octogenarian senator’s early support for the Green New Deal and so-called “Medicare for all” also helped win him the support of younger Dems.
On the campaign trail, Markey hammered Moulton over his critical comments about how Democrats approach the issue of transgender males playing in female sports.
The senator accused Moulton of throwing “trans kids under the bus,” for stating back in 2024 that he didn’t want his young daughters “getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete” and suggesting Democrats are afraid to take on the issue.
Moulton, however, seemed to walk back his position during a debate earlier this month.
“I think they should,” he said, when asked if transgender athletes should be allowed to take part in girls’ sports, adding that there should be “a discussion” about “issues of safety and fairness.”
In his victory speech, Markey described his win as a “testament to the power of the progressive movement … fueled by young people.”
Meanwhile, Moulton pledged to “do everything I can to help [Markey] win re-election in November.”
“Challenging the establishment and calling for a new generation of leadership isn’t easy, but it is necessary,” the congressman said in a statement, vowing to “continue to push the Democratic Party – and our country – to look towards the future.”
In the crowded Democratic primary race for the North Shore House seat being vacated by Moulton, former Biden White House official Dan Koh emerged victorious.
Koh, who previously served as deputy assistant to former President Joe Biden and deputy director of the White House Office of Intergovernmental Affairs, topped state lawmaker Tram Nguyen and the rest of the 6th District primary field with 42.3% of the vote.
In the Massachusetts gubernatorial race, incumbent Gov. Maura Healey ran unopposed in the Democratic primary.
Healey, who is seeking a second term, will face businessman Mike Minogue, the winner of Tuesday’s Republican primary, in November.
In another generational challenge in the Bay State, 77-year-old Rep. Richard Neal (D-Mass.) beat 39-year-old Jeromie Whalen in Massachusetts’ 1st Congressional District Democratic primary.
Neal, who is seeking a 20th term in the House in the solidly blue district, won by a 55% to 45% margin.

sources.news_title: Markey fends off generational challenge and other Massachusetts primary takeaways
sources.text:
Sen. Ed Markey will win the Democratic nomination for US Senate in Massachusetts, CNN’s Decision Desk projects, fending off a primary challenge from Rep. Seth Moulton as he seeks a third full term.
In a year that has seen the ouster of several veteran Democrats at the hands of younger candidates running to their left, 80-year-old Markey cast himself as the more, progressive anti-establishment option in his showdown with Moulton, a six-term congressman who has bucked party leadership at times.
“Tonight is a testament to the power of the progressive movement,” Markey told supporters at the historic Omni Parker House in Boston Tuesday night. “It is a progressive movement fueled by young people, demanding more from their leaders, and it’s your voices that are the ones we need to hear right now.”
“Generational change isn’t about compromising to do the small things better. It’s about fighting to do the big things best,” he added.
It was one of several key nominating contests in deep-blue Massachusetts that tested voters’ appetite for change at a time when the party base is widely dissatisfied with congressional Democrats’ efforts to oppose President Donald Trump. By and large, however, they opted to stick with the status quo.
The road to the 2026 midterms starts now

In the Boston-based 8th District, the race mapped more neatly along the ideological and generational fault lines animating this primary season, with CNN projecting that moderate Rep. Stephen Lynch, who entered Congress in 2001, will defeat a well-funded, and three decades younger, challenger running to his left.
Meanwhile, in the crowded Democratic race to succeed Moulton in the 6th District, CNN projects that Biden White House alum Dan Koh will win the primary, overcoming anti-establishment sentiment.
Here are the key takeaways from Tuesday’s primaries:
Markey overcomes a generational change message
While Moulton, 47, argued that the time had come for Markey, who first joined Congress in 1976, to make way for new leadership, he was unable to convince voters.
The two clashed sharply on the subject at debates, with Moulton seizing on Markey’s recent stumble while fielding a question about AI regulations. “This is why we need a new generation of leaders to regulate these technologies,” the congressman said.
But Markey pushed back on that criticism, telling CNN over the weekend, “I’ve always been the youngest guy in the world when it comes to ideas,” as he embraces resistance to the Trump administration. And he appealed to progressives in the liberal Massachusetts electorate, drawing contrasts with Moulton while pointing to his support for the Green New Deal, “Medicare for All” and transgender rights.
Markey told supporters Tuesday evening that he had spoken with Moulton and congratulated him on a “hard fought campaign.”
Markey now advances to the general election as the favorite to retain his seat in the reliably blue state against Republican John Deaton. If reelected, the senator says he will not seek a fourth term.
Moderate Democrat fends off challenge from the left
Lynch, 71, defeated 39-year-old Patrick Roath, an attorney and voting rights activist who campaigned on a message of generational change and staked out more progressive policy positions.
In his campaign, Roath called for reducing the cost of childcare and healthcare, congressional term limits, and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement. He clashed with Lynch over the incumbent’s voting record on immigration and healthcare.
Roath outraised the incumbent, bringing in close to $1.3 million for his campaign as of mid-August, according to Federal Election Commission filings, while Lynch brought in about $900,000.
But Lynch overcame the fundraising disadvantage and will be heavily favored to retain his seat, which represents parts of Boston and its suburbs, in November.
A Biden-Harris endorsement wins out
Koh, a former deputy Cabinet secretary and special assistant to President Joe Biden, was bolstered by endorsements from his old boss and former Vice President Kamala Harris.
He also leaned on his local ties, highlighting his service as chief of staff to former Boston Mayor Marty Walsh, who later became Biden’s labor secretary, and as a member of the city of Andover’s select board.
Koh focused his campaign on lowering the cost of living, protecting democracy and supporting universal healthcare.
While some rivals sought to criticize his establishment ties, Koh consolidated local and national support to secure the nomination for the northeast Massachusetts seat, which is open following Democratic Rep. Seth Moulton’s decision to run for Senate.
Koh is favored to win the general election for the historically blue seat against Republican Micah Jones, who ran unopposed in the GOP primary.
This story has been updated with additional race projections.
CNN’s Arlette Saenz contributed to this report.

sources.text:
Massachusetts Sen. Ed Markey easily won the state’s Democratic primary on Tuesday night, dispatching a younger and more moderate challenger in a significant victory for the party’s progressive wing.
Markey defeated Rep. Seth Moulton, a decorated veteran of the war in Iraq who had long been tipped as a rising star in the party but struggled to turn his potential into lasting political impact. Moulton, age 47, had made his comparative youth a major part of his campaign against Markey, who has served in Congress for nearly 50 years and will be 86 when his Senate term ends in 2032.
The race was shaping up as a blowout: With about half of the votes counted around 10:30 p.m. Eastern, Markey held a 65% to 35% lead over Moulton. Markey’s margin of victory was likely to easily surpass his performance in 2020, when he defeated former Rep. Joe Kennedy III in another primary centered around age and generational change.
Like in his race against Kennedy, the party’s progressive wing rallied behind Markey, a reliable liberal who has closely aligned with Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and is known for his emphasis on combating climate change. Warren, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) appeared together in a campaign ad for Markey.
While Markey’s victory is a clear win for the left, results elsewhere in Massachusetts did not present a clear narrative. Dan Koh, a former official in President Joe Biden’s administration who ran with the backing of Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris, won the primary to replace Moulton in Congress.
Koh, who held senior non-editorial roles at HuffPost more than a decade ago, was considered the moderate option in the primary as progressives rallied behind state Rep. Tram Nguyen.
Two other races between younger progressives and veteran establishment members of the House remained too close to call.
Recent surveys had shown Markey pulling away from Moulton, who had won his seat in Congress more than a decade ago by successfully defeating Rep. John Tierney in a primary to win a seat representing the Boston suburbs on the state’s North Shore.
Moulton’s military credentials ― the Boston Globe once famously revealed he had actually underplayed his achievements ― made him a closely watched figure on Capitol Hill. But he made an ill-conceived challenge to then-Democratic leader Nancy Pelosi following the 2018 elections and followed it up with a flop of a presidential campaign in 2020.
Democratic voters’ anger and desire for generational change following the political failure of an octogenarian president seemingly gave Moulton a fresh opening to do what Kennedy could not six years earlier.
Moulton, however, was a rare candidate to mount a generational change challenge from the party’s center. While not an avowed centrist, Moulton is generally skeptical of the party’s far left and questioned whether Democrats’ stance in support of allowing transgender children to play sports cost the party the 2024 presidential election.
Markey and his allies pounced on those comments, using them to question whether Moulton would reliably stand up for progressive principles, and Moulton ultimately apologized for them.
“I am confident that because of this campaign, others will be inspired to buck the system when they are told to wait their turn,” Moulton said in a speech after he conceded to Markey.
Markey is set to face Republican John Deaton, an attorney closely associated with the cryptocurrency industry, in November. The race is considered safely Democratic.

sources.text:
Democratic Sen. Ed Markey defeated Rep. Seth Moulton in the Senate primary in Massachusetts, NBC News projects, in a victory for the party’s progressive wing.
Markey was winning about two-thirds of the vote percentage points with 69% of the expected vote reporting.
Markey’s win comes as other longtime Democratic lawmakers have lost to younger challengers in primaries this year. But the 80-year-old senator fended off his challenger by touting his liberal record as an author of the Green New Deal and vocal supporter of “Medicare for All.”
“It’s all about not just sending a Democrat to the Senate — it’s sending a progressive Democrat to the Senate from Massachusetts so there can be someone that reflects your values every single day,” Markey said at a rally on the eve of the primary, describing the race as “a progressive final round.”
Moulton said Tuesday night that he had called Markey “to congratulate him on his victory tonight.” Moulton told supporters that Markey “has my full support as our Democratic nominee, and we must stand united this November to protect our democracy and defeat Donald Trump.”
Moulton and his allies had a spending advantage in the race, spending $7.1 million on ads to Markey and his allies’ $3.9 million, according to AdImpact. That makes Markey’s win another victory for a progressive who faced an onslaught of well-funded attacks.
On the campaign trail and the airwaves, Markey also touted endorsements from progressive leaders, including Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who both appeared in an ad for the senator, and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York.
Moulton, the 47-year-old congressman, called in his campaign for generational change — a call that has cost a handful of House Democrats their seats in primaries across the country this year. Markey was first elected to the Senate in 2013 after serving nearly 40 years in the House.
“Sen. Markey and I want the same things, but wanting isn’t winning, and the old way isn’t working,” Moulton said in one of his TV ads, listing policies including “tax the oligarchs, abolish ICE, pass healthcare for all.”
But Markey and his allies attacked Moulton for his past criticism of liberal policies. Commonwealth Together PAC, an outside group that has attacked Moulton, launched an ad saying the congressman opposes Medicare for All and taxing billionaires, pointing to 2019 comments from Moulton’s unsuccessful campaign for president.
Markey also sharply criticized Moulton on transgender issues, saying at the election-eve rally that Moulton “threw trans kids under the bus” after the 2024 election. Moulton told The New York Times after Democrats lost the presidential race: “I have two little girls. I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete, but as a Democrat I’m supposed to be afraid to say that.”
Moulton apologized to “anyone hurt by those comments” in a recent debate.
In his primary campaign, Markey also vowed to continue fighting President Donald Trump.
“It’s a moment in history where Trump is challenging everything that started right here 250 years ago,” Markey said in one ad, referring to the country’s founding. “We have a message from Massachusetts: We are going to fight.”

sources.news_title: Incumbent Sen. Ed Markey wins Massachusetts' Democratic primary for U.S. Senate
sources.text:
Incumbent Sen. Ed Markey wins Massachusetts' Democratic primary for U.S. Senate
Sen. Ed Markey has won the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate in Massachusetts, according to a race call by The Associated Press, repelling a challenge from Rep. Seth Moulton.
While the result marks yet another win for the progressive wing of the party this election cycle, it's also a defeat for those calling for generational change and a new direction in party leadership.
Loading...
In other recent primaries, races have been fought across generational lines with younger Democratic candidates running as progressives, challenging older incumbents sometimes arguing that it's time for new ideas.
Yet Markey successfully fought off discontent among Democrats with their party's establishment by arguing that he has long fought for progressive ideals.
Markey, who turned 80 this July, first became a congressman in 1976. Moulton joined politics more than three decades later, in 2014, and has repeatedly called for a new generation of leadership through the race.
Sen. Markey, who often introduces himself as the son of a milkman from Malden, supports "Medicare for All," and raising taxes on the rich, while opposing President Trump's defense budget.
He believes that the focus of candidates' debates should be on their ideas and not their age.
"This is the most energized I've ever been, fighting Donald Trump every single day, fighting his agenda to undermine families all across our country," Markey said during a debate hosted by WWLP in July. "And I lead that fight."
Markey had been leading the polls recently, which also revealed that his supporters felt a connection to his progressivism and were less moved by concern over his age.
The senator had endorsements from his fellow senator from Massachusetts, Elizabeth Warren, as well as Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York.
In an August debate, Markey accused Moulton of not standing up for transgender rights, telling the congressman that after President Trump was reelected, "You threw those trans kids under the bus."
He was referring to when Moulton in 2024 said Democrats should be able to talk about trans issues, adding that he didn't want his daughters "getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete."
During the debate, Moulton apologized for hurting people with his comments and said he supports LGBTQ rights.
This was the second time Markey won a primary challenge against a much younger candidate. In 2020, Markey defeated Rep. Joe Kennedy III, who also argued that Massachusetts needed younger representation.
Markey will now face attorney John Deaton this November for the Senate seat.
Markey is heavily favored to win come November in deep blue Massachusetts.

Incumbent Rep. Richard Neal, 77, has defeated teacher Jeromie Whalen, 39, in the Democratic primary for Massachusetts 1st Congressional District, DDHQ and NBC News project.

With this win, he’ll almost certainly serve a 20th. No Republican is running in the November general election.
The 1st District covers the western and some central parts of the state, including the city of Springfield.

Polls closed for the Massachusetts primary at 8 p.m. ET. Results are expected shortly.

- 2024: 16.7%
- 2022: 21.75%
- 2020: 36.58%
- 2018: 21.85%
- 2016: 8.84%

Andrew Walters voted for incumbent Sen. Ed Markey at the Somerville Public Library West Branch on Tuesday, saying that he "knew Markey" and that the incumbent is "a strong Democrat."
Walters recognized that age was an issue for Markey but that he was the better choice in the race over Rep. Seth Moulton.
“I think his ideologies are pretty good; he’s definitely getting up there,” he said. “I didn’t see a clear younger progressive candidate that I would have voted for instead.”
Walters added that he does not think the country is going in the right direction. "I’d like to see more people stand up to Trump and stop ICE,” Walters said.

A few more eyes were watching voters when New Bedford Election Commission Chair Manuel DeBrito Jr. visited the Buttonwood Warming Place senior citizen center Tuesday as he made the rounds of several polling places in the Massachusetts coastal city.
In July, the Justice Department announced that election monitors would be sent to New Bedford for the Sept. 1 state primary due to problems concerning "the integrity of elections." However, the agency did not give any examples of problems.
"We’re running around as we usually do, just making sure people know what they can do as far as observers," DeBrito Jr. said. "We want to make sure everyone gets in to vote."
About an hour south of Boston and 30 minutes from Providence, Rhode Island, New Bedford is located in Bristol County along Buzzards Bay in Massachusetts' South Coast region.
In a July 8 post on X, Assistant Attorney General for the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division Harmeet Dhillon said New Bedford was one of 15 jurisdictions in six states getting election monitors. In 2024, complaints were made during the March 5 Super Tuesday presidential primary election in New Bedford. However, an investigation found the problems were minor, and they had no impact on the results.
There are always observers, DeBrito Jr. acknowledges, but there are more in this primary than usual. Federal observers are also present this year, though the election chair said they didn’t tell local officials exactly where they would be.

One of Democratic figures keen on the Sept. 1 contest in Massachusetts is former DNC Vice Chair David Hogg, who exited the party last year after clashing with leadership over primary endorsements.
Hogg's group, dubbed Leaders We Deserve, has been supporting many of the younger primary challenges this year including Patrick Roath, 39, over Stephen Lynch, 71, in the state's 8th congressional race that covers the southeastern part of the state.
The group has spent about $470,000 support Roath, according to federal campaign finance records.
In an Aug. 27 virtual town hall, he explicitly called for term limits when saying many of the problems facing the country, such as affordability, will require younger Millennials and Gen Z candidates to run.
"I think it means having some new people step up into these roles and run, if you're young especially," Roath said.
Several online posts by Hogg, a survivor of the 2018 Parkland, Florida high school shooting, emphasized the three decade age gap between the two rivals. The gun control activists also decried Lynch for accepting corporate PAC money and for being the last House Democrat in office who voted against the Affordable Care Act in 2010.
Brockton voter says 'age is just a number'

Marlon Roberts cast his ballot at Gilmore Elementary School in Brockton Tuesday morning. The 53-year-old said the main race that got him out to the polls was the U.S. Senate Democratic primary between incumbent Ed Markey and Rep. Seth Moulton.
“I went with Markey because he knows what he is doing,” Roberts said. “He’s been in Congress a very long time.”Roberts said he wasn’t concerned about Markey’s age becoming a factor in his ability to serve.
“Age is just a number,” he said. “Once you’re doing a good job, I believe that you deserve to be in office.”
Robert’s said there weren’t any local races that stood out to him on the ballot, so he primarily turned out to vote with interest in the Senate race.
“I had to make sure (Markey) goes there, in Congress,” he said.
Democrats have mixed results over age in earlier primaries
Phillip M. Bailey
So far in the 2026 primary season at least five congressional Democrats – from Texas to Colorado – who are age 65 or older have lost to younger foes amid the anti-establishment revolt.
Most recently 78-year-old Rep. John Larson, of Connecticut, was defeated by former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, 47, in August. That race turned into a referendum on who had the energy to resist President Donald Trump's administration.
But in four other contests where Democratic incumbents are above retirement age they have beat back their challengers, including 78-year-old Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Mississippi, who easily defeated Evan Turnage, a 34-year-old antitrust lawyer, by a whomping 74 percentage points in March.
Voter: 'I don't want people who are 80'
Sue Scheible and James Powel
Kathleen Brown told The Patriot Ledger, a part of the USA TODAY Network, she voted for Rep. Seth Moulton due to concerns over the ages of elected officials.
"I don’t want people who are 80 and who will be 86 in office to be in office. They are too old for leadership positions," the 53-year-old retired data analyst said after voting at the Tirrell Room in Quincy.
Moulton has made age a central attack line against incumbent Sen. Ed Markey in the Democratic primary in a season that has seen older incumbents knocked out of long-held seats by younger challengers.
John and Lenore Grazioso, both 86, also voted at the Tirrell Room, an event hall about 10 miles southeast of Boston.
They said they vote mainly because they always have and feel strongly it is their civic duty. They are trying to convince others to also keep voting, too.
Trump administration sent election monitors to MA
Margie Cullen
The U.S. Justice Department is monitoring polls in Boston, Lowell and New Bedford, Massachusetts, the Civil Rights Division announced Sept. 1.
According to a press release, the DOJ sent 12 monitors to polls in those three cities.
“Monitoring is an essential duty for the Civil Rights Division during election season,” Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division said in a statement. “Nonpartisan, nondiscriminatory monitoring efforts promote transparency, accountability, and most importantly trust in our federal elections.”
This primary season so far, the department has deployed over 80 monitors to 200 polling locations across eight states, including Arizona, Michigan and Minnesota, and is planning on sending monitors to New Hampshire and Virginia, according to a post Dhillon made in July.
In that post, Dhillon said election monitors were being sent “to places where there have been problems with the integrity of elections.” Dhillon did not get into specific instances of “problems” for any of the jurisdictions.
While there were complaints made during the March 5 Super Tuesday presidential primary election in New Bedford in 2024, an investigation found the problems to be minor and had no effect on results.
It isn’t so unusual to have election monitors at the polls: according to the MA Secretary of the Commonwealth’s office, it’s typical for the DOJ to send monitors to cities and towns with language requirements under the Voting Rights Act.
However, New Bedford has no such requirements.
Who might replace Seth Moulton in MA 6th District?
Margie Cullen
Six Democrats are on the ballot for the Massachusetts 6th Congressional District seat being vacated by Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., who is running for U.S. Senate. This district encompasses the Northeast part of the state.
Among the candidates are former White House official Dan Koh, 41, and state Rep. Tram Nguyen, 40.
Koh has received endorsements from former President Joe Biden, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Boston mayor Marty Walsh.
Nguyen has received endorsements from U.S. Democratic Reps. Ayanna Pressley and Lori Trahan, MA Attorney General Andrea Campbell and the Boston Globe.
UMass Boston political science professor Erin O’Brien said that Koh has been tagged with “the more moderate DC swagger, DC insider,” while Nguyen and others have been seen as “progressive, not as connected, grassroots.”
The outcome of the race, she said, will signal what “flavor of Democrat” voters are looking for.
“I don't know if the frame's completely fair, but the frame that's been put on this race is more moderate, DC connections, more of an outsider, which one of those will make a difference?” O’Brien said. “It's one data point on what direction is the Democratic Party going.”
The other candidates include software engineer Bethany Andres-Beck, 42, businessman John Beccia, 56, and Topsfield Town Moderator Jamie Belsito, 52. Former federal worker Mariah Lancaster, 36, ended her campaign on Aug. 30 and endorsed Nguyen. There has been limited polling in the race.
A solid blue district, the winner of the primary is expected to win the general election.
What to know in MA governor race
Margie Cullen
Democratic Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey is uncontested in the Democratic primary. But she will face a general election challenge from one of two Republicans vying for the nomination.
The candidates in the Republican primary are Michael Minogue, former CEO of a medical device company, and Brian Shortsleeve, former MBTA chief administrator. The two are fairly similar: they are both military veterans turned businessmen who support cutting taxes and immigration enforcement.
However, Minogue does not support abortion rights, while Shortsleeve does. Minogue also leads handily in fundraising, with $8.1 million on hand compared to Shortsleeve's about $527,000 according to the latest campaign finance reports.
Has Trump endorsed any candidates in Massachusetts?
Margie Cullen
President Donald Trump has stayed out of the Massachusetts races, not endorsing any candidates this cycle.
In the past, he has. In 2022, he endorsed former Massachusetts state Rep. Geoff Diehl, R-Whitman, in his 2022 run for governor. Diehl won the primary but lost the election to Gov. Maura Healey.
So far this election cycle, Trump has a near-perfect record when it comes to endorsing winning Republican primary candidates: a 96% success rate in GOP contests across congressional, state legislative and statewide elections so far in 2026, according to a review of Trump’s picks by Ballotpedia.
Challengers stress generational change in contested primaries for US House
Margie Cullen
All of Massachusetts nine House seats are considered safe Democratic seats. But the current representatives face more primary challenges than usual this year, with many revolving around generational change.
Here are the contested Democratic primaries:
1st Congressional District: Incumbent Richard Neal, 77, vs. Jeromie Whalen, 39, a teacher. This district covers the western and some central parts of the state, including the city of Springfield.
4th Congressional District: Incumbent Jake Auchincloss, 38, vs. Jason Poulos, 40, an AI researcher. This district goes from communities right outside Boston, like Newton and Brookline, down to the Rhode Island border and Fall River.
5th Congressional District: Incumbent House minority whip Katherine Clark, 63, vs. Tarik Samman, a 27-year-old union organizer and Harvard Law School researcher, and Jonathan Paz, a 33-year-old former Waltham city councilor and immigrant rights organizer. This district includes suburbs north and west of Boston, including parts of Cambridge.
6th Congressional District: Six Democrats are vying for the seat vacated by Rep. Seth Moulton, who is running for Senate. They are software engineer Bethany Andres-Beck, 42, businessman John Beccia, 56, Topsfield Town Moderator Jamie Belsito, 52, former White House official Dan Koh, 41, former federal worker Mariah Lancaster, 36, and state Rep. Tram Nguyen, D-Andover, 40. This district encompasses the Northeast part of the state.
8th Congressional District: Incumbent Stephen Lynch, 71, vs. Patrick Roath, a 39-year-old lawyer and former aide to former Gov. Deval Patrick. This district includes parts of Boston, its suburbs and southeast Massachusetts.

The other candidates were software engineer Bethany Andres-Beck, 42; businessman John Beccia, 56; and Topsfield Town Moderator Jamie Belsito, 52. Former federal worker Mariah Lancaster, 36, was on the ballot but ended her campaign Aug. 30 and had endorsed Nguyen.
Rep. Bill Keating wins in 9th District
Margie Cullen
Incumbent Rep. Bill Keating, 73, has defeated Craig Swallow, a 40-year-old consultant, in the Democratic primary for Massachusetts’ 9th Congressional District, which covers Cape Cod and the Islands and parts of the South Shore, DDHQ and NBC News project.
The race was one of the many in Massachusetts that revolved around generational change. Keating has served eight terms in the House.
With this win, he’ll likely serve a ninth. He will face Republican R. Tyler MacAllister, who was uncontested in the Republican primary, in November in the solid blue district.
Moulton hopes his campaign inspires new leadership
Terry Collins
Rep. Seth Moulton, who was soundly defeated by incumbent Massachusetts Sen. Ed Markey for the Democratic Senate nomination, said he hopes his campaign run will inspire others seeking newer and younger leadership.
During a brief concession speech at his campaign party in Dorchester, Moulton said he congratulated Markey, but was disappointed that "the outcome isn’t what we wanted to achieve."
"I could not be prouder of the fight we put up," Moulton said, thanking his family and supporters in defeat. "We ran a race that stood on principle and not about politics as usual."
Markey was leading Moulton by nearly a 3-to-1 margin at one point when the Associated Press and NBC News called the race about 30 minutes after polls closed.
Moulton told supporters he knew he was an underdog and that "calling for a new generation of leadership isn’t easy, but it is necessary." To cheers, he added that he would "not stop challenging the Democratic Party and the country to look for new leadership."
He said while he is proud of the work he's done in Congress, many Americans still "remain disillusioned with the status of our country," and there is far more work to do.
Moulton concluded that he hopes that, because of his campaign, "others will be inspired to buck the system when they are told to wait their turn."
House Minority Whip Katherine Clark defeats two challengers
Margie Cullen
House Minority Whip Katherine Clark will defeat two challengers in the Democratic primary for Massachusetts’ 5th Congressional District to win an eighth term in the U.S. House, NBC News and DDHQ project.
She bested Tarik Samman, a 27-year-old union organizer and Harvard Law School researcher, and Jonathan Paz, a 33-year-old former Waltham city councilor and immigrant rights organizer.
Clark will almost certainly win the general election as no Republicans are running in the 5th District, which includes suburbs north and west of Boston and parts of Cambridge.
Rep. Jake Auchincloss fends off AI researcher in MA 4th District
Margie Cullen
Incumbent Rep. Jake Auchincloss, 38, has defeated Jason Poulos, a 40-year-old AI researcher, in the Democratic primary for Massachusetts’ 4th Congressional District, NBC and DDHQ project.
He will face Thomas Stalcup, who was unopposed in the Republican primary, in the November general election. Like all nine House districts in Massachusetts, the district is rated “Solid D” by the Cook Political Report.
Incumbent Gov. Maura Healey to face Minogue in governor race
Margie Cullen
Michael Minogue, a 59-year-old businessman and inventor, has defeated Brian Shortsleeve, a former MBTA administrator, in the Republican primary for Massachusetts governor. The Associated Press and Decision Desk HQ called the race around 8:45 p.m. ET.
Minogue will face incumbent Gov. Maura Healey, who was uncontested in the Democratic primary.
The Cook Political Report rates the race “Solid D.”
Markey defeats Moulton
Margie Cullen
Sen. Ed Markey has defeated Rep. Seth Moulton in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate, NBC News and the Associated Press projected shortly after polls closed Tuesday, all but assuring the longtime senator a third full term.
Moulton, 47, had run on a message of generation change, arguing that Markey, 80, was too old for another term and that the state needed a new generation of leaders. However, Markey had stressed the benefits of his experience and as well as his progressive credentials.
“It’s not your age, it’s the age of your ideas,” he said repeatedly on the campaign trail.
On Tuesday, it appeared Markey’s message had won out.
Markey will face Republican John Deaton in the general election in November. However, in the safe blue seat, Markey is expected to win.
Polls close in Massachusetts
James Powel
Polls closed for the Massachusetts primary at 8 p.m. ET. Results are expected shortly.
What is voter turnout looking like in MA? Comparison to historical data
Margie Cullen
Over 10% of Massachusetts residents already voted before polls even opened on Sept. 1.
According to the Secretary of the Commonwealth’s office, 555,525 people had cast their ballots for the Massachusetts primary election early, with 483,946 returning a ballot by mail and 71,579 voting early in person.
It’s the highest in-person early voter turnout the state has had for a primary since 2020, Deb O’Malley, director of communications for the office, said in an email.
Turnout for primary elections tend to be fairly low. In 2024, the overall turnout, including both early voting and day of voting, in the primary was just 16.7%.
The highest percentage in recent years was 36.58% in 2020, when Sen. Ed Markey, D-Massachusetts, faced a high-profile challenge from then Rep. Joe Kennedy, D-Massachusetts.
Here is the turnout percentage in the past five state primary elections in Massachusetts, based on data from the Secretary of the Commonwealth's Elections Division:
- 2024: 16.7%
- 2022: 21.75%
- 2020: 36.58%
- 2018: 21.85%
- 2016: 8.84%
Somerville voter chooses Markey even though 'he’s definitely getting up there'
Fernando Cervantes Jr.
Andrew Walters voted for incumbent Sen. Ed Markey at the Somerville Public Library West Branch on Tuesday, saying that he "knew Markey" and that the incumbent is "a strong Democrat."
Walters recognized that age was an issue for Markey but that he was the better choice in the race over Rep. Seth Moulton.
“I think his ideologies are pretty good; he’s definitely getting up there,” he said. “I didn’t see a clear younger progressive candidate that I would have voted for instead.”
Walters added that he does not think the country is going in the right direction. "I’d like to see more people stand up to Trump and stop ICE,” Walters said.
More observers than usual at one Massachusetts polling site
Frank Mulligan
A few more eyes were watching voters when New Bedford Election Commission Chair Manuel DeBrito Jr. visited the Buttonwood Warming Place senior citizen center Tuesday as he made the rounds of several polling places in the Massachusetts coastal city.
In July, the Justice Department announced that election monitors would be sent to New Bedford for the Sept. 1 state primary due to problems concerning "the integrity of elections." However, the agency did not give any examples of problems.
"We’re running around as we usually do, just making sure people know what they can do as far as observers," DeBrito Jr. said. "We want to make sure everyone gets in to vote."
About an hour south of Boston and 30 minutes from Providence, Rhode Island, New Bedford is located in Bristol County along Buzzards Bay in Massachusetts' South Coast region.
In a July 8 post on X, Assistant Attorney General for the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division Harmeet Dhillon said New Bedford was one of 15 jurisdictions in six states getting election monitors. In 2024, complaints were made during the March 5 Super Tuesday presidential primary election in New Bedford. However, an investigation found the problems were minor, and they had no impact on the results.
There are always observers, DeBrito Jr. acknowledges, but there are more in this primary than usual. Federal observers are also present this year, though the election chair said they didn’t tell local officials exactly where they would be.
David Hogg tests Gen Z power in MA 8th congressional district
Phillip M. Bailey
One of Democratic figures keen on the Sept. 1 contest in Massachusetts is former DNC Vice Chair David Hogg, who exited the party last year after clashing with leadership over primary endorsements.
Hogg's group, dubbed Leaders We Deserve, has been supporting many of the younger primary challenges this year including Patrick Roath, 39, over Stephen Lynch, 71, in the state's 8th congressional race that covers the southeastern part of the state.
The group has spent about $470,000 support Roath, according to federal campaign finance records.
In an Aug. 27 virtual town hall, he explicitly called for term limits when saying many of the problems facing the country, such as affordability, will require younger Millennials and Gen Z candidates to run.
"I think it means having some new people step up into these roles and run, if you're young especially," Roath said.
Several online posts by Hogg, a survivor of the 2018 Parkland, Florida high school shooting, emphasized the three decade age gap between the two rivals. The gun control activists also decried Lynch for accepting corporate PAC money and for being the last House Democrat in office who voted against the Affordable Care Act in 2010.
Brockton voter says 'age is just a number'
Janson McNair
Marlon Roberts cast his ballot at Gilmore Elementary School in Brockton Tuesday morning. The 53-year-old said the main race that got him out to the polls was the U.S. Senate Democratic primary between incumbent Ed Markey and Rep. Seth Moulton.
“I went with Markey because he knows what he is doing,” Roberts said. “He’s been in Congress a very long time.”Roberts said he wasn’t concerned about Markey’s age becoming a factor in his ability to serve.
“Age is just a number,” he said. “Once you’re doing a good job, I believe that you deserve to be in office.”
Robert’s said there weren’t any local races that stood out to him on the ballot, so he primarily turned out to vote with interest in the Senate race.
“I had to make sure (Markey) goes there, in Congress,” he said.
Democrats have mixed results over age in earlier primaries
Phillip M. Bailey
So far in the 2026 primary season at least five congressional Democrats – from Texas to Colorado – who are age 65 or older have lost to younger foes amid the anti-establishment revolt.
Most recently 78-year-old Rep. John Larson, of Connecticut, was defeated by former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, 47, in August. That race turned into a referendum on who had the energy to resist President Donald Trump's administration.
But in four other contests where Democratic incumbents are above retirement age they have beat back their challengers, including 78-year-old Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Mississippi, who easily defeated Evan Turnage, a 34-year-old antitrust lawyer, by a whomping 74 percentage points in March.
Voter: 'I don't want people who are 80'
Sue Scheible and James Powel
Kathleen Brown told The Patriot Ledger, a part of the USA TODAY Network, she voted for Rep. Seth Moulton due to concerns over the ages of elected officials.
"I don’t want people who are 80 and who will be 86 in office to be in office. They are too old for leadership positions," the 53-year-old retired data analyst said after voting at the Tirrell Room in Quincy.
Moulton has made age a central attack line against incumbent Sen. Ed Markey in the Democratic primary in a season that has seen older incumbents knocked out of long-held seats by younger challengers.
John and Lenore Grazioso, both 86, also voted at the Tirrell Room, an event hall about 10 miles southeast of Boston.
They said they vote mainly because they always have and feel strongly it is their civic duty. They are trying to convince others to also keep voting, too.
Trump administration sent election monitors to MA
Margie Cullen
The U.S. Justice Department is monitoring polls in Boston, Lowell and New Bedford, Massachusetts, the Civil Rights Division announced Sept. 1.
According to a press release, the DOJ sent 12 monitors to polls in those three cities.
“Monitoring is an essential duty for the Civil Rights Division during election season,” Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division said in a statement. “Nonpartisan, nondiscriminatory monitoring efforts promote transparency, accountability, and most importantly trust in our federal elections.”
This primary season so far, the department has deployed over 80 monitors to 200 polling locations across eight states, including Arizona, Michigan and Minnesota, and is planning on sending monitors to New Hampshire and Virginia, according to a post Dhillon made in July.
In that post, Dhillon said election monitors were being sent “to places where there have been problems with the integrity of elections.” Dhillon did not get into specific instances of “problems” for any of the jurisdictions.
While there were complaints made during the March 5 Super Tuesday presidential primary election in New Bedford in 2024, an investigation found the problems to be minor and had no effect on results.
It isn’t so unusual to have election monitors at the polls: according to the MA Secretary of the Commonwealth’s office, it’s typical for the DOJ to send monitors to cities and towns with language requirements under the Voting Rights Act.
However, New Bedford has no such requirements.
Who might replace Seth Moulton in MA 6th District?
Margie Cullen
Six Democrats are on the ballot for the Massachusetts 6th Congressional District seat being vacated by Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., who is running for U.S. Senate. This district encompasses the Northeast part of the state.
Among the candidates are former White House official Dan Koh, 41, and state Rep. Tram Nguyen, 40.
Koh has received endorsements from former President Joe Biden, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Boston mayor Marty Walsh.
Nguyen has received endorsements from U.S. Democratic Reps. Ayanna Pressley and Lori Trahan, MA Attorney General Andrea Campbell and the Boston Globe.
UMass Boston political science professor Erin O’Brien said that Koh has been tagged with “the more moderate DC swagger, DC insider,” while Nguyen and others have been seen as “progressive, not as connected, grassroots.”
The outcome of the race, she said, will signal what “flavor of Democrat” voters are looking for.
“I don't know if the frame's completely fair, but the frame that's been put on this race is more moderate, DC connections, more of an outsider, which one of those will make a difference?” O’Brien said. “It's one data point on what direction is the Democratic Party going.”
The other candidates include software engineer Bethany Andres-Beck, 42, businessman John Beccia, 56, and Topsfield Town Moderator Jamie Belsito, 52. Former federal worker Mariah Lancaster, 36, ended her campaign on Aug. 30 and endorsed Nguyen. There has been limited polling in the race.
A solid blue district, the winner of the primary is expected to win the general election.
What to know in MA governor race
Margie Cullen
Democratic Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey is uncontested in the Democratic primary. But she will face a general election challenge from one of two Republicans vying for the nomination.
The candidates in the Republican primary are Michael Minogue, former CEO of a medical device company, and Brian Shortsleeve, former MBTA chief administrator. The two are fairly similar: they are both military veterans turned businessmen who support cutting taxes and immigration enforcement.
However, Minogue does not support abortion rights, while Shortsleeve does. Minogue also leads handily in fundraising, with $8.1 million on hand compared to Shortsleeve's about $527,000 according to the latest campaign finance reports.
Has Trump endorsed any candidates in Massachusetts?
Margie Cullen
President Donald Trump has stayed out of the Massachusetts races, not endorsing any candidates this cycle.
In the past, he has. In 2022, he endorsed former Massachusetts state Rep. Geoff Diehl, R-Whitman, in his 2022 run for governor. Diehl won the primary but lost the election to Gov. Maura Healey.
So far this election cycle, Trump has a near-perfect record when it comes to endorsing winning Republican primary candidates: a 96% success rate in GOP contests across congressional, state legislative and statewide elections so far in 2026, according to a review of Trump’s picks by Ballotpedia.
Challengers stress generational change in contested primaries for US House
Margie Cullen
All of Massachusetts nine House seats are considered safe Democratic seats. But the current representatives face more primary challenges than usual this year, with many revolving around generational change.
Here are the contested Democratic primaries:
1st Congressional District: Incumbent Richard Neal, 77, vs. Jeromie Whalen, 39, a teacher. This district covers the western and some central parts of the state, including the city of Springfield.
4th Congressional District: Incumbent Jake Auchincloss, 38, vs. Jason Poulos, 40, an AI researcher. This district goes from communities right outside Boston, like Newton and Brookline, down to the Rhode Island border and Fall River.
5th Congressional District: Incumbent House minority whip Katherine Clark, 63, vs. Tarik Samman, a 27-year-old union organizer and Harvard Law School researcher, and Jonathan Paz, a 33-year-old former Waltham city councilor and immigrant rights organizer. This district includes suburbs north and west of Boston, including parts of Cambridge.
6th Congressional District: Six Democrats are vying for the seat vacated by Rep. Seth Moulton, who is running for Senate. They are software engineer Bethany Andres-Beck, 42, businessman John Beccia, 56, Topsfield Town Moderator Jamie Belsito, 52, former White House official Dan Koh, 41, former federal worker Mariah Lancaster, 36, and state Rep. Tram Nguyen, D-Andover, 40. This district encompasses the Northeast part of the state.
8th Congressional District: Incumbent Stephen Lynch, 71, vs. Patrick Roath, a 39-year-old lawyer and former aide to former Gov. Deval Patrick. This district includes parts of Boston, its suburbs and southeast Massachusetts.

Ed Markey beats Seth Moulton, to win Democratic nomination in Massachusetts' Senate primary
Markey defeats Moulton in U.S. Senate primary
sources.text:
Support WBUR
Markey defeats Moulton in U.S. Senate primary
U.S. Sen. Ed Markey has won Tuesday's Democratic primary, according to a race call from The Associated Press. The veteran progressive fended off a challenge from U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton, who had called for a new generation of leadership.
Markey, 80, who has served in Washington since before Moulton, 47, was born, will face Republican John Deaton in November.
In his victory speech Tuesday night, Markey called the win a "testament to the power of the progressive movement of our nation" and nodded to the age factor, saying the movement was "fueled by young people demanding more from their leaders, and it's your voices that are the ones we need to hear right now. Your leadership will show us the way."
At a time when many older members of Congress are being swept out of office by younger, more progressive candidates, Markey ran as a leader of his party's progressive wing against Moulton, who is more moderate on some issues. Markey is the oldest senator Massachusetts has ever elected and the oldest Senate Democrat seeking reelection this year. But throughout the primary, he argued that he was "more energized than ever."
"I'm always the youngest guy in the room when it comes to new ideas," he told WBUR the week before the primary.
Markey co-sponsored the Green New Deal and backs Medicare for all, and he was endorsed by leading progressives, including U.S. Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders, and U.S. Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ayanna Pressley. He also was endorsed by a number of progressive groups, including the Sunrise Movement and College Democrats of Massachusetts.
Moulton, who launched his Senate campaign last October, has repeatedly argued that Markey, who would be 86 at the end of his next term, "is too old."
"I think that we need to learn the lessons of Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Dianne Feinstein and Joe Biden," Moulton told WBUR. "I believe it's time for a new generation of leadership to take on Trump and lead us forward.”
But voters on the left weren't ready to give up on Markey. And on Tuesday night, in a concession statement, Moulton said, "I spoke to Senator Markey tonight and pledged that I will do everything I can to help him win re-election in November, to ensure a Democrat represents the state we both love."
While the two agreed on most policy issues, Moulton returned again and again to Markey's age, arguing that his "decision to cling to power” puts progressive priorities at risk. He, along with The Boston Globe, which endorsed Moulton, suggested that because of his age, Markey might not be able to finish his next term.
Markey pushed back, arguing that if he couldn't do the job he would step down: "The same thing should be true for Congressman Moulton. It should be true for anyone," he said.
Markey, who grew up in Malden, where his father drove a truck for the Hood milk company, said he's more determined than ever to oppose President Trump.
"Donald Trump brings out the Malden in me every day — and I fight him every day." he told WBUR.
While Democrats in several states debate whether to embrace progressives or moderates, Massachusetts, for now, seems willing to send left-leaning veterans to the Senate. Markey in particular has spent decades burnishing his reputation as a leader of the state's progressive establishment.
He benefited from the support of voters like Chris Trapper, of Westwood, who said he appreciated Markey's long experience and his leadership on climate issues.
"He's always been a leader and a progressive before it was kind of cool," Trapper said.
This is the second time Markey has fended off a primary challenge across generational lines; six years ago he defeated U.S. Rep. Joe Kennedy III, who also argued that it was time for a new generation of leadership.
In a deep blue state, Markey will be heavily favored in the race against the Republican, Deaton, who lost his first bid for the Senate two years ago against Warren. Massachusetts hasn't sent a Republican to Congress since Scott Brown's stunning upset victory in 2010 following the death of U.S. Sen. Ted Kennedy.
This segment aired on September 2, 2026. The audio for this segment is not available.

US Sen. Ed Markey wins Massachusetts Democratic primary over opponent who called for change - Boston News, Weather, Sports
sources.text:
Related
U.S. Sen. Ed Markey secured the Democratic nomination in Massachusetts’ Senate primary for his reelection bid Tuesday, once again fending off a push for generational change as he seeks a third term.
Markey, 80, defeated U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton, 47, who argued that it was time to do away with the “status quo.”
Markey successfully pointed to Moulton’s more moderate positions to argue that it was Moulton — not the older incumbent — who was out of touch with the state’s voters.
Markey had boasted about his 2022 climate bill and called for an end to the war in Iran to bring down energy costs. He also sharply criticized Moulton for opposing “Medicare for All” — though Moulton called for universal healthcare.
“He has a backwards-looking political agenda,” Markey said.
In heavily Democratic Massachusetts, the primary is considered the most critical election hurdle, and the winner is expected to prevail in the general election in November.
Markey has been a fixture in Massachusetts politics since the 1970s, prompting Moulton to make his “status quo” arguments on the campaign trail and to question Markey’s accomplishments during his lengthy time in office.
In a concession speech, Moulton said he would now support Markey.
“Challenging the establishment and calling for a new generation of leadership isn’t easy. But it is necessary,” Moulton told supporters. “We started conversations that needed to happen.”
“We didn’t achieve our goal tonight, but I am confident others will be inspired to buck the system when they’re told to wait their turn,” he added.
The Senate race was not the only generational challenge for Democrats on Tuesday’s ballot. A similar dynamic played out in the 8th Congressional District, where Patrick Roath hoped to oust longtime incumbent Rep. Stephen Lynch, and in the 1st Congressional District of western Massachusetts, where progressive public school teacher Jeromie Whalen faced against Rep. Richard Neal.
Moulton’s comments on transgender children were an issue
During the campaign Markey repeatedly pointed out that Moulton, in 2024, raised eyebrows among some in the party for saying he did not want his daughters playing sports against transgender girls.
Critics said he was echoing President Donald Trump’s talking points against allowing transgender athletes in girls’ and women’s sports.
Moulton later apologized for his remarks, saying it was not his intention to hurt the transgender community and stressing his support for other transgender rights bills.
“If you’re in the trans community or you’re a trans kid feeling the weight of the Trump administration and the Supreme Court, you matter,” Moulton said during an August debate. “You’re valued, and I will always have your back.”
Moulton, who enlisted in the Marines after the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, and served four tours of duty in Iraq, was first elected to Massachusetts’ 6th Congressional District in 2014. He launched a 2020 presidential campaign but dropped it after a few months.
Markey was elected to the Senate in 2013. Before that he represented Massachusetts’ 7th Congressional District from 1976 to 2013.
Markey notably fended off a challenge in 2020 from Rep. Joe Kennedy III, a younger rival from one of the nation’s most famous political families. Markey did so by aligning himself with the liberal wing of the Democratic Party.
Antoine Hilaire, a 76-year-old Democrat who voted for Markey in Brockton on Tuesday, said being older can be a positive because it offers people experience and wisdom.
“If the older one is doing the better job, I don’t know,” he said. “He’s doing a good job. It’s not a big, big, big problem.”
Longtime Democratic House incumbents also face younger challengers
Lynch, 71, has held the 8th District seat in south Boston since 2001. He faced Roath, a 39-year-old lawyer who contended that it is time to end “wait-your-turn” politics. Lynch stressed the value of experience inside Congress.
Lynch has fended off other youth challenges in the past, but Roath’s campaign hoped for a boost of excitement after longtime Democratic incumbent U.S. Rep. John Larson was defeated by former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin in August in neighboring Connecticut. Like Roath, Bronin called for the need for generational change while running against an establishment politician.
Meanwhile the 1st District primary in western Massachusetts pitted Neal, 77, against Whalen, 39.
Neal, known as the dean of the New England House delegation, was first elected in 1988. Whalen ran to the left of Neal, calling for Medicare for All and questioning whether Neal has done enough to oppose Trump’s agenda.
Whalen recently was endorsed by Our Revolution, a progressive organization founded by Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont.
___
Associated Press reporter Leah Willingham in Brockton contributed.

U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton carried all six Marblehead precincts Tuesday in the Democratic U.S. Senate primary, even as Sen. Ed Markey won decisively statewide to secure his party’s nomination for another term.
Moulton received 2,894 votes in Marblehead, compared with 1,876 for Markey, giving the congressman a 1,018-vote advantage in town. Eight write-in votes were also recorded.
Among Marblehead voters who selected either candidate, Moulton received 60.7% of the vote, while Markey received 39.3%.
Statewide, the result went strongly in the opposite direction. Markey received 557,022 votes, or 64.9%, compared with Moulton’s 301,135 votes, or 35.1%. Markey finished 255,887 votes ahead of Moulton across Massachusetts.
Marblehead, which Moulton has represented in Congress as part of the 6th Congressional District, backed him in every precinct.
Moulton received 566 votes in Precinct 1, 479 in Precinct 2, 375 in Precinct 3, 507 in Precinct 4, 474 in Precinct 5, and 493 in Precinct 6.
Markey received 362 votes in Precinct 1, 348 in Precinct 2, 298 in Precinct 3, 260 in Precinct 4, 292 in Precinct 5, and 316 in Precinct 6.
Moulton’s largest advantage came in Precinct 4, where he received 507 votes to Markey’s 260, a difference of 247 votes.
The contest was closest in Precinct 3, where Moulton received 375 votes to Markey’s 298, a margin of 77.
Moulton’s highest raw vote total came in Precinct 1, where he received 566 votes. Markey also recorded his highest total there, with 362.
The two candidates received a combined 4,770 votes in Marblehead. With eight write-ins, 4,778 votes were cast for a candidate in the Senate race. Another 44 ballots were left blank, bringing the total number of Democratic ballots represented in the precinct results to 4,822.
Moulton conceded the race Tuesday night and said he had spoken with Markey and pledged to support him in the general election.
“We entered this race as an underdog and know the outcome tonight might not be what we had hoped for,” Moulton said. “We ran a race that stood on principle — that wasn’t just about politics as usual — and that elevated the voices of Massachusetts citizens who have been left behind by the status quo in Washington.”
Moulton, who gave up his 6th Congressional District seat to challenge Markey, centered his campaign in part on generational change in Democratic leadership.
“Challenging the establishment and calling for a new generation of leadership isn’t easy, but it is necessary,” Moulton said. “I will continue to push the Democratic Party — and our country — to look towards the future.”
Despite the contentious primary, Moulton said he would now work to help Markey keep the Senate seat in Democratic hands.
“I spoke to Senator Markey tonight and pledged that I will do everything I can to help him win re-election in November, to ensure a Democrat represents the state we both love,” Moulton said.
Markey, meanwhile, celebrated his victory before hundreds of supporters at his election-night headquarters in Boston and credited young voters and the progressive movement with delivering the nomination.
“Tonight is a testament to the power of the progressive movement,” Markey said. “It is a progressive movement fueled by young people demanding more from their leaders.”
Markey also responded to the generational argument that had become a central theme of Moulton’s campaign.
“Generational change isn’t about compromising to do the small things better; it is about fighting to do the big things the best,” Markey said.
Marblehead was one of the places where Moulton’s campaign produced a markedly different result from the statewide outcome. He finished more than 1,000 votes ahead of Markey in town and won every precinct, with margins ranging from 77 votes in Precinct 3 to 247 in Precinct 4.
But the local advantage was not enough to overcome Markey’s support across Massachusetts, where the incumbent took nearly 65% of the Democratic primary vote and advanced to the November general election.

sources.text:
Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., defeated Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., in Tuesday’s Massachusetts Democratic Senate primary, turning back a younger challenger who made generational change a central theme of his campaign, as reported by Fox News.
The Associated Press projected Markey as the winner less than an hour after polls closed on Sept. 1, 2026. The victory puts Markey, 80, on track to seek another full term in the U.S. Senate after nearly five decades in Congress.
Moulton, who is 47, had made Markey’s age and the need for a new generation of Democratic leadership major parts of his campaign.
Despite that challenge, Markey held onto the Democratic nomination by emphasizing his progressive record and strong ties to the party’s left wing.
The race also highlighted a significant divide within the Democratic Party over transgender athletes and participation in sports.
Markey has continued to openly support transgender rights during the 2026 midterm campaign, including allowing transgender athletes to participate in sports.
“Trans athletes should be able to play,” Markey told The New York Times. “That reflects Massachusetts and who we are. And Seth Moulton does not.”
Moulton had previously taken a different position, arguing that Democrats paid a political price by avoiding the issue.
He said the party’s reluctance to address concerns about biological sex and women’s sports contributed to Democratic losses in 2024.
“I have two little girls, I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete, but as a Democrat I’m supposed to be afraid to say that,” Moulton said at the time.
The disagreement placed the two Massachusetts Democrats on opposite sides of an issue Republicans have repeatedly used on the campaign trail.
Democrats nationally have generally been less vocal about transgender sports policies as they work to regain control of Congress.
Markey’s victory also represents a win for prominent progressives. The Massachusetts senator has long been associated with the Democratic Party’s progressive wing and co-authored the Green New Deal resolution.
During the primary campaign, Markey received endorsements from progressive figures including Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.
The outcome also comes amid a larger debate inside the Democratic Party over age and leadership.
Calls for generational change intensified following the political turmoil surrounding former President Joe Biden and his effort to seek a second presidential term.
Several longtime Democratic incumbents have faced younger challengers in recent election cycles. In one notable example, Rep. John Larson, D-Conn., 78, lost to Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, 47.
Moulton attempted to make a similar case in Massachusetts, arguing that the party needed new leadership.
His defeat means Markey will remain the Democratic standard-bearer for the Senate race in a state where Democrats have maintained a strong political advantage.
Massachusetts has not elected a Republican senator since 2013, when former Sen. Scott Brown lost his reelection bid to Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass. Given the state’s political makeup, Markey’s positions are unlikely to pose a significant obstacle to his expected November campaign.
After conceding the primary, Moulton said his challenge had been about more than defeating one incumbent. He argued that confronting longtime Democratic leaders was necessary for the party’s future.
“Challenging the establishment and calling for a new generation of leadership isn’t easy, but it is necessary. I will continue to push the Democratic Party — and our country — to look towards the future,” Moulton said in a statement.
Markey’s win is also not his first victory over a younger Democrat in a primary centered partly on generational change.
In 2020, Markey defeated former Rep. Joe Kennedy III in the Massachusetts Democratic Senate primary.
Kennedy, a member of the Kennedy political family, had challenged Markey in an effort to win the nomination and represent a younger generation of Democratic leadership.
